GIVE EVERY MON HIS DUE. .„.,„,„..„! - Aw've rambled up an' deawn this waurld. For fivean' sixty year'; Aw've booath hed monyXmerry laugh, An' mony a lonely tear; Aw'm one 'at knows both friends:an' foes; There's lots o' things aw rue: I But this is still ml motto, lads : Give every mon his due. Ov cooarse, when aw wer green an' young, Like mony a lad beside, Aw use/ to think this waurld knew o, An' bowed befoor id pride; But soon aw fun' that iv a chap Wer poor as weel as true, 'Twere ten to one, though hard he toyled, He'd never ged his due. Yo see there's sich a lot o' fooak 'At's bad one graclelre'e— Thegy peep an' smile at th' rich an' fine, But th' poor they conned see.: They'll like a mon iv he geds on, An' joyns their empty crew: But iv he does his best an' fails, - They think no praise is due. There's some fooak laughs when t' weather's fine, An' cosses when id rains—l Them's um as likes the men wi' brass, But scorns the men wi' brains. There's mony a chap gies o Ins peawrs To help his neighbours through, But, like the rain that feeds the fleawers, He seldom geds his due. When dark an' deadly slander comes To cleawd a mon's good name, There's awlus lots o' idle tongues o gpreyd th' unwelcome fame. But give to me the kindly sowls— Aw wish they waurnd so few— That patient bide, watch every side, An' give the mon his due. 0 mates! i' country place an' teawn, Through t' length and breadth o' t' land, There's many a lonely heart breyks deawn Witheawt a helpin' hand. But let coodwill be near us still, When others' fotes we view; For One aboon 'II render soon To every mon his due! , Higher Walton, Nov. 23rd, 1838. GEORGE HULL.

Designing men.—Architects. Nothing but leaves.—A pamphlet. Doing light work.--Cleaning the lamps. The moment a man is satisfied with himself:everybody di,* is dissatisfied with him—Arab Proverb. To have a respect for ourselves guides our'morals ; and to have a deference for otherl governs our,manners.— Sterne. To ensure long life recreation should i be apart of our daily life. It makes the busy man thoughtfui and the theughtful man busy. It ensures health,fsuccess, and the'accomplishment in less time of more and better work. Young lady at seaside (to mariner): "Why are :all vessels spoken of as ' she?' It's because they glide so gracefully—now, isn't it?" Mariner: "No, miss, it ain't. It's acause of their riggin' costing so much." Fond Mother: "Wellit.Bessie, now that you have seen your cousin Walter, what do you think of him? Did he le.ave a pleasant impression ?" Bessie: "Oh, yes, mamma; be kissed me." "The next time you send delicacies to my wife," re- marked the mendicant, "I wish you wouldn't send any more jam. "Nor' "No, please send some jelly?" "Doesn't your wife like jam?" "Yes, but I don't." ,-•'-r1 "So your old uncle is dead, Charley ?" "Yes, (Fed yesterday." "He was a very eccentric old fellow. Do yon think he was altogether right in his head?" "Welt —er—l couldn't say, you know, until the will is read." Certainly "man's wicked `angel is In money*: :I often catch myself with something bold as a lionLbouncing from my. heart when the shillinerattles,'and the lion, as small as any weasel, slinks back ag,ain:when the shilling is gone.—D. Jerrold. A young lady, after listening to her lover's description of the setting sun, exclaimed, "Oh, Alphonse! Alphonse! what a soul you have for art! You were meant for a great 'painter !" Her father unexpectedly close behind them added, "and glazier!" Mrs. Chilsley : "I see statistics show that 75 per cent. of male criminals are unmarried." Mr. Chilsley : "Which shows how many men prefer the penitentiary to matri- mony." And the ensuing silence was so deep that Mrs. Chilsley could hear herself reflect. "West, John, how are you to-day?" said a minister to one of his parishioners on meeting him on the road. " Gey vreel, sir; gey weel," replied 'John, cautiously, "gin it wisna for the rheumatism in inyi richt leg." "Ali, well. John, be thankful, for there is no mistake you are getting old, like the rest of us, and old age, you know, doesn't come alone." "Auld age, sir," returned John; "I won'er to hear ye. Auld age has naething to do wit Here's my Wier leg, jist as auk], an' it's quite soonil an' soople yet." GOINO HOME Faint TIIR livcruns.—Young Theologian: "Miss Buxom, are you not oppressed with a sense of your own insignificance when You gaze up into the blue vault above us, and think of you myriads of whirling worlds that encompass this little globe of ours? And when you dwell on the considerations of eternity, and the infinity of spade, do you not experience an uncon- querable:&earning for more knowledge, greater capa- city of intellect, and a clearer comprehension of those stablime mysteries in the spiritual and material universe, which all our most earnest mental efforts so miserably fail to penetrate ?" Miss B.: ""Welt, no, Mr. Surplice. I have not been 'oppressed with a sense of my own insignificance' since; I was weighed tat Uncle Fred's store last month ;:and I never ' experienced unconquer- able yearnings' except when dinner is late." And his disappointment was larger than the Grand Central depot.

_ NOT AN INSIDE PASSINGP.D.—A capital story is told of a dentist whose stature is not in keeping with his pro- fessional capabilities. In fact, h 0 is so far below the average height that he has had to erect a sort of plat- form in front of the chair in which his patients sit while undergoing the agonising process of having their teeth extracted. He was visited recently by a man of ' the giant-agriculturalist type, who wished to get rid of a tormenting tooth. The dentist invited him to the "torture chair," and then climbed on to the platform already mentioned. When the patient beheld this he ' opened his mouth to a width which would have put a ne,gro to the blush, and seeing that he still continued straining himself to increase the opening if possible, the dentist patted him on the shoulder, and, with Assuring calmness, said, "Don't exert yourself, my man, for I'm going to remain outside." AUTHORS' WlVES.—Wivee have been eyes, hands, mind, and everything to their husbands. The great authority on "Bees "—Huber, a Geneva naturalist—was blind from his seventeenth year, and yet he found means to master a branch of natural history demanding the closest observation and keenest eyesight. It was through the eyes of his wife that his mind worked as if they had been his own. She encouraged her husband's studies as a means of alleviating his privation, which, at length, he came to forget. We have all read in the biography of the late Professor Fawcett how his wife was eyes to him also. After twenty-eight years' experience, Faraday spoke of his marriage as "an event which more than any other had contributed to his earthly happiness and healthy state of mind." For forty-six years the union continued unbroken, the love of the old man remaining as fresh, as earnest, and ai heart-whole as in the days of his youth. Another man of science, Tames Nasmyth, the inventor of the steam-hammer, had a similar happy ex- perience. "Forty-two years of married life," he said, "finds us the same devoted • cronies' that we were at the beginning." Perhaps authors, more than any other class of famous men, have been indebted to their wives. 'Torn Hood had such confidence in his wife's judgment that he read, and re-read, and corrected, with her, all he

wrote. Many of his articles were first' dictated to her, and her ready memory supplied him with referenoes and quotations. Anthony Trollope said that no person but his wife had ever read a line of his manu- script, "to my very great advantage in matters of taste." The French writer, Alphonse Daudet, had deter- mined to temain a bachelor, because he was afraid that if he made a wrong step in marriage he might dull his imagination; hut, on being introduced to Mademoiselle Julie Allard, who loved literature, and was a charming writer and critic herself, his fear was removed. The union proved a very happy one, and the picture of the two at work is an attractive bit of biography, "She has been," says his brother, 'the light of his hearth, the regulator of his work, and the discreet counsellor of his inspiration. There is not a page that she has not re- vised, re-tcuchea, and enlivened; and her husband has 1), male Otitness to te? ilevotion an 4 c 91.131,- Ation in the dedication of 'Nabob,' but she would not allow this dedication to appear." Once, it is related, he had a sentimental and dramatic scene with his wife, con- cerning which he remarked, "This seems, my dear, like a chapter that has slipped out of a novel." "It is more likely, Alphonse," was the reply, "to form a chapter that will slip into one." Wives, like Mrs. Carlyle, have as- sisted their husbands' work by keeping house so well that their indigestions and tempers were not unneces- sarily disturbed. Hawthorne acknowledged that the /Inspiration which produced his imperishable contribu- Orions to American classics depended foi its undisturbed flow on a serene and happy domastic erwirontnerlii, which •-;is wife alone could supply.—Cassell's Family Mayagine. FATAINS (presents from the fair). Aw've a nebbur as olez meks a practice o' buyin' his childer fairing, an it's a varragood practice, too, only aw wish he'd vary aid bit; id is too bad to buy th' lads (an' ther's six on 'em) everyone on 'em a drum apiece. A balloon, or a spy'glass wodn'd be quite as noisy, an' wed suit 'em just as wee!. Just thee try id, nebbur ! FRATCH (praise‘. To hatch o' onybody i' these parts meeans to praise 'em, bud aw've nooatist fro' readin' Ben Brierley's werks as fratch meeans just th' opposite . . _ . . .

i' some places, thad is foin' eawt, an to'rt Blackpoo' rooad id nieeans Fo (fall). Th' payson sed as this meant th' Devil, an' aw sed "th' Dickens id does !" Aw towd him as we sed "Pride mon hey a fo," an' lie sed as id owt to hey a lot o'fou,'Sooa aw up an' towd Mtn as heaw mony Id hed th' Devil wodn'd be one. FBEETEND, FLAYED (frightened). An' he sed as &yin' a chap wer' skinnin' him! Well, freetenin' him's quite as bad; bud thee is a lot o' chaps as is thad "thick skinned" id wod tek a lot to flay 'ern. FAIN (glad). Then be rambled on an' sed as fain

, meant pretendin', bud aw med wod they co a pun, an aed as when a chap wor fain he wer' to fain to feign. Focrriss (footings). This is nowt bud an excuse for a spree. When a chap (generally a tackler) sterts at a new place he pays his footins, thad is, summat to'rt . .

a spree; a lot moor join in, an' they bey' a " pmto- pie do" at a pub. They olez sup abeawt a flat pint o' beer to ev'ry spoonful o' pie; heaw they find ther way hooam is a mystry to me. FLUDIMOXT (puzzled, upset). This word doesn'd otezmeean this, bud, nine times eawto'ten, id isn't' far eawt on't. FIRE POYT This is nayther moor nor lees nor a pooaker to stor th' fire up wi'. FUDDLED drunk). Ther's two sooarts as geds fuddled— men an' wimmen, an' they o act quite different when tber thad state; some on 'em goes in for thumpin' evry body they meet, whether it's a bobby or Cher wife, an' Callers go hooam an' give o'th' childer 'apeunies, an' act gradely soft o reawnd. For (fetch). "Aw'll fot thee a welt o' chops,' a clp once sed to _ me, an' aw sed "0 reet; tha con fa: id, . _ _ _

bud dorn'd be in a hurry bringin' id." . Fizzoa (face). Yo' o know wod a fizzog is beawt bein' towd bi me. FOOTRO football). Aw know a tocothri i' Lancashire as hes mony a time paid as mich as eighteenpence to gooa an' watch a footbo match; they've ceawrd theer moor nor two heawrs th' cowdest day i' winter, i' drizzlin' rain, watchin' a lot o' lazy young fellas punse one another's legs. An' them as hes paid ther brass hes lied a wife an' childer at hooam hofe-clamd. Yo' may offer 'ern good books at a penny apiece, or grand picters at th same price, or eheeap lecters, or owt else, but they'll hey nowt to do wi 'em; they'd rayther see a Blegburner knock a Prestoner deawn ony day, soon as they con tawk abeawt id at after—for months an' months. FAIISE (old-fashioned, knowihg). Id used to be sed as id wer a fause child as knew ad own fayther. They kessen a child fause iv id geds jealous (All' new babby, bud just let that child be fause enuff to find th' rooad to wheer th' toffy's kept, an' hill ged wod for. FLAY-CROW (scarecrow). Tiler's different sooarts o'

flay-crows 'to wod yo' see-i' corn fields; slob as Lasses wi' big bussels, an' lads wi' their mustaches med as sherp as stockin' needles, etsetra. Fon (further): When a gossipy nebbur's wife says heel be gpoin' for," id. doesled olez meean as boo's for

bi king chalk. FIFITLE (condition, to mend). To fettle a thing meeans to mend id, bud aw het) beard fooak say as fettled ale isn'd much mended. [New (ugly, ill-favoured). Aveye heerd some nice lasses co' one another fence, when they werefoin'eawt o'er th' same young fella, an' nayther on 'Pm thowt as they wer' tellin' a rateher. FELLA (a man). A W'M a fella bud my', partner isn'd much o' one—aw meenn my Celia, partner, nod my psrtner as aw'm wed to, though hoo wants to wear

'ern at times. Foo' (fool). Id id easy te be a foe', neaw-a-days. Yo've only to gooa fuddlin', an' th' teetotallers tell yo' yo're a foo' ; or yo' dorn'd gooa fuddlin', an' th' drunken chaps co' yo' a (ye' know wed sooart) foo'. Yo' con bet on hosses an' footbo' matches, or play :penny "nap" at tb' club, or put yo'r brass i' building societies, or owt o' thad acoart, an' yo'll soon hear feoaks' opinion on ye'. "An' tha may get Mad name for varra little," aw sed to th' payson. "Aw heard a varra intelligent chap say as tha wer' a too' for preychin' nearly a heawr last Sunda' neet—tha mon be keerful, lad." DOMESTIC ECONOMY: OR, WIVES AND HUSBANDS. 1 (From "Lays and Lyrics," by GEO. LANCASTER, Hull.) PART IT. The chill October eve begins to drive, And the last bee has sought his easy hive. Fast sinks the sun, the crimson fades away, Departing daylight sheds a fainter ray. No more the forms of lovers are descried Linked in sweet couples by the river side ; No more the angler, with expectant eye, Upon the water casts the gaudy fly: The misty streets are full of gloomy damps, And the lamplighter bastes to light his lamps. • Beams in the upper story shine afar From Lila's dressing-room—l mean boudnir. 'Tis there she braids her hair and tints her face, Transfigured daily in that lofty place. Now gentry sleep, the hour their habits fix, Who lunch at two, and dine at half-past six. Now ladies weep o'er novels inltheir rooms, How mighty heiresses elope with grooms, And noble houses sink beneath 'a curse. And high-born babes are deftly changed at nurse, And lowly maids are wooed by princely swains, And sleeping kings have pins run through their brain, And levers agonies are safely passed, . Ending in matrimonial bliss at last. The anxious Lila had prepared the tea, And nursed a little cherub on her knee. A snow-white garment, stiff with starch and lace, Adorned the babe, and scrubbed its little face; And over this—well washed, sad tucked, and wide To keep it clean—a pinafore was tied. Then a fair bib, and yet one covering more,. ,To shield the bib, the robe, and pinafore. Riche), her friend, to have a social chat, Had just run in, and on thessofa eat. Poor, troubled Lila begged her friend to play, To chase the clouds of doubt and care away. No longer able to refuse, she went . And sat majestic at the instrument; There, proudly conscious of her power to please, She skipped her fingers lightly o'er the keys— Now up, now down. The gamut softly whirls Among the trebles like a string of pearls; Then swift descending to the thundering base, Roared like a lion in the trembling case, Which echoing ended with a massive chord Or two clipped short.. Again the ivory board Rains Semitones, as her white fingers pass, Like hailstones blown upon the frozen glass By winter blasts, and tapering to soft shades Of liquid music, quivering with roulades And quaintest modulations, without seeming care To make divisions; slides into an air That the young Tyrolean shepherd trills To black-eyed lasses on the Ithetian Hills. At first, in dancing bars it trips along, / Then the notes trailed pathetically long, As if the jilted lover wept and prayed For smiling glances from the heartless maid. Rachel, a tear on Lila's face perceives; To chase the tear away, she interweaves A pretty passage of melodious thirds, Like to the concert of two cuddie birds. Amongst the keys her fingers:wandered sweet And soft as any caterpillar's feet. Then, rising on a sudden, as if shot, She said—" Excuse me, Lila, I forgot ' To leave with Isabel the store-room key. And there's no sugar for my husband's tea. Good-bye, my dearest Lila." Then she bent To kiss the baby, and.away she went. On Lila's face there still remained a cloud, And tears would *tart as thus she spoke aloud : " Why does my truant husband stay so late? He never, never caused the tea to wait Like this before, since first ho married me. Fool, that I was, to use my tongue so free, And drive him furious from his pleasant home, In search of kinder folks perhaps to roam. Oh! had I kept resigned to cook-maid's toil, And been content to stew, to bake, to boil, This disagreement never had been bred, Nor had, alas! these bitter tears been shed. Till this sad morning, was there one young bride In all the town, more unrestrained beside? Where was there one so favoured, and so free, So petted, fondled, and beloved as me? With what a generous husband was I blest, Who ne'er denied a moderate request, Or made a single hindrance to my will, Or swore an oath, or grumbled at a bill. What shows, what concerts to my share did fall; Nay, scarce a month went past without a ball. And, oh! to think, when pleasures were supreme, Whorl all my days were one delightful dream Of meetings past, and projects yet to come, At White's, at Brown's, at Rachel's, and at home; That fate, or chance, or be it what it may, Should bring such sudden changes in a day." She spoke, and sighing, spread before her face A muslin kerchief, edged with pointed lace. soft floating odours permeate the room, And grief is soothed with smells of rich perfainae. And now she starts, for hem footsteps fall, And hollow knocks resound within the hall— (The entrance—such 'twas Lila's pride to call). In stalks Dick Horner with a hasty tread, Who, seeing Lila, thus abruptly'said— " We found your husband in the river—dead." At this, the lady groaned three dreadful " Oh's," And down she sunk, oppressed with shocking woes. Dick caught her fainting ere she struck her head. -And bore hey all unconscious to a bed; There laid her gently down with decent care, Repressed a laugh, and slowly came down stair. Meanwhile poor Robin had absolved the dirt, And doffed a wet, and donned a drier shirt, Then soon prepared as drownod and deceased, To lie in state, a day or two at least. "Now let the room," he cried, "be warm, I pray, And bring refreshments slyly in the day; Good cuts of beef, and draughts of cheery-wine, Nor ever place hard boards beneath my spine, To stretch the bones on such an aching rack, Let downy pillows prop my weary back. And do them, Dick, my worthy, trusty friend, Observe my wife, and all her ways attend, And when she camas, as come I know she will, Give me good, notice to lie straight and still; A day's repose will me, perhaps, restore, And I may live to bless the world once more. Go, Richard, go, and watch till Lila wake, And bid her rally for the baby's sake." Straight, Dick obeys, to Lila's couch be hies, And thus, with well affected sorrow cries "Rise, lady, rise, and moderate thy pain, Thy husband's dead, thy child, thy friends remain To claim thy smiles. and I shall thinkme blest, If I may be accounted with the rest, To soothe thy grief, to mitigate thy tears, And be a prop to thy remaining years. Grief such as this will death or sickness bring. Recall the words of Israel's shepherd king. His baby died, but dal he grieve? Not he. Can tears and fasting bring him back to me?' (Thus said the King) 'Then I will cease to mourn, For I may go, but he will not return.'" From Lila's eyes afresh the fountains broke, Which, with the sheets, she dried, and thus she spoke: "Thy manly words are stays to my despair, They cheer my heart, and half remove the care. Thus the frail sapling, riven by the storm, Against the sturdy oak supports its form. Even now my soul, obedient to thy voice, Will make a feeble effort to rejoice." Straight she arose, Dick tenderly attended, Fo arm in arm they both at once descended. Nay, blame not reader, reader do not blame, If queries soft in Lila's mind there came, Which turned her night of tears to cheerful day, And chased or reasoned all her grief away. Why should she thus to maddest grieving fall, About a husband dead beyond recall? Why should she be hysterically sad One husband lost—another may be had? To-day, sincerely she was Robin's mourner, Ere long she might be Mistress Richard Horner. But Dick, it was a most depraved intent, To give these thoughts so much encouragement. When souls like these thus play a subtle pare, With interest and with mischief at the heart, When each contends to draw the other out, How fast the ripening friendship comes about! For now, at Dick's request, the table's spread, Reluctant Lila to a seat is led. Not much they ate, hut very long they sat, And spent an hour, at least, in pensive chat— Familiar like; but ere they said the grace, An awful pallor came on Richard's face. Be rolled upon the floor; he groaned and cried— ' " Oh! lam dying! Oh, my side, my side !" "Good God !" shrieked Lila, "what a luckless day. , My husband—now my friend is snatched away. Not all the heroes of the new romances Have been convulsed with more o'erwhelming chances. Will nought assauge? Will nought thy life restore? Or hast thou never felt these pains before?" "Yes, oft," gasped Dick, "and nothing gives repose Except—except—a dead—a dead Iran's nose." Here, Lila raised her hands above her head. "Good heavens ! a dead man's nose," she groaningsaid, "Good heavens! and does humanity require 2" "I faint,' gasped Dick again, "1 sink—expire."' Away ran Lila, nor a moment lingers, And snatched a raz r in her fitful fingers, To pillage her dead husband of his nose, So up the stairs with flying feet She goes. It can't be wrong, she thought,: he cannot smell, So he won't want it, aini if Dick gets well-- , Why should I hesitate, or fear, or falter 2 She thought again; her mind began Walter; For well he knows in history who ranges, • The human mind is prone to sudden changes. Judas, for coin, his Master did betray. ..e And then he rued, and flung the coin away. 'Twas so with Lila: when she reached the door, She dashed the razor on the chamber floor, And thus broke out in thie hysteric burst:—.
THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 1,1888. HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
THE FAILURE OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Bank- ruptcy Court, Peter Sinnott, of New Ferry, late of Runcorn. appeared before the Registrar (Mr. Nicholson) to undergo his adjourned public exam- ination. The larticulars of the bankruptcy have previously been published in the "Examiner." The Official Receiver (Mr. C. J. Dibb) said that the bankrupt had been ordered to file certain account*. He had just handed in a statement to him (Mr. Dibb) to the effect that he was Unable to give a statement of his affairs, as he had not kept books, or any record of his affairs. He had not kept any- thing from the creditors, but had to the best of his knowledge given them the truth of his affairs. He also declared that he was left penniless. That state- ment, Mr. Dibb said, was not one that could be justi- fied. Before, when he had an interview with Mr. Sianett, shortly after a receiving order was made, the bankrupt had somewhat anticipated the inquiries that would be made and in a book he had he professed to make some sort made, of monies he had received, and how they had been expended. In his public exiunin- ation the debtor said that he had a banking account, and that considerable portions a his money were paid through that. When he said, therefore, that he had no records of cash receipts or cash payments that was not the fact. The examination had been adjourned in order that inquiries might be made with regard to the pro- perty the bankrupt was dealing in when the judgment for costs was given against him in the action with the Railway Company. He (Mr. Dibb) had submitted the result of the inquiriee in regard to the property to the solicitor acting on behalf of the Railway Company, who agreed with him that there had been dealings with property that were unjustifiable. At the same time, to recover the property would mean embarking upon costly litigation, and it was to be feared that what was recovered would be overbalanced by the costs incurred. There were no funds in hand, and the Board of Trade did net think it part of their duty to provide funds for the purpose of obtaining assets for creditors. The Railway Company did not wish to send good money after bad It had transpired that so late as the 15th of September, some months after the receiving order was made, the bankrupt bad actually received £l5 on the equity of a life policy, which he never disclosed. Altogether, he thought he was justified in saying that the bankrupt had had but one intention since the judgment was obtained against him, , and that was to deprive the Railway Company by every means in his power of .he awards of the judgment. Mr. Dibb ventured to Isubmlt that the debtor had committed a misdemeanour under the Deluters' Act, by the way in which he had dealt with his property. He thought that the best way would be to adjourn the examination sine die. He did not 'propose to prosecute the debtor, as he thought it might be a sufficient penalty if he did not have his discharge. He could not apply for his discharge until he had purged himself of contempt of court, which he had incurred by 'not filing accounts.—The Registrar told the bankrupt that he might thank his stars that a different applieation had not been made on the aubject. He (the debtor) had placed himself in a very dangerous position by the course that he had adopted. Be had no doubt disobeyed the court, and was open to committal at any time.—The examination was then adjourned frt:::e die.

CHAPTER XXIIj, AFTER THE "WINE!'

The spectacle which greeted Ursula's eyes was even more painful than Fielding had anticipated. Raymond's rooms were beautifully furnished, the cloture*, china, and decoration of the walls, the ex- quisitely-toned drapery, and the carved oak furniture were perfect; Ray still revelled in the oysters and Chablis of Art. .An American organ was open, some oratorio music of liandel's stood on it; Ray had cared more than ever lately for the great master in wathetic way, and could strum a little when he was in the mood.

But he was now extended on the 'sofa apparently asleep. Fielding had no difficulty in grasping the situation. During the last few days by the doctor's orders he had been keeping the alcohol from him, but taking advantage of the short absence of the friend who had been watching over him, the unfor tunate lad must have Stolen from the sofa, and helped himself to some cognac. Probably it had been secreted in a hiding-place only known to himself. The liqueur case stood by his sido ; the odour of brandy WA in the room.

Ursula stepped ttis to him, laying her cool hand gently on the tangle of hair which was now histreless and dank, stroking thq ;sallow cheeks from which the rich curves of healthy, youth had disappeared. " He- has been very ill," she said. "Yes, he has been very ill. They were quite un- able to move him."

, And then the sick man looked up with the beautiful violet eyes-90 like his mother's,an d from which it was natural to expect such great things. He showed that he was aware of his sister's presence by a little convulsive movement, and then he threw off her hand with.an oath; covering his face with his out- stretched fingers. Her own face was white and full of pain, as she averted her eyes from Fielding's sor- rowful gaze. Never before had Raymond spoken brutally to his sister' but Fielding had feared some outbreak of this sort. He felt that he must-cope with it, though to do so might be to bring upon himself Ursula's anger. He knew that there was no evil influence to which Raymond might not succumb if his sister could not help him. Her nature was such a thoroughly healthy one,that even now his weaker one might be braced by hers. No doubt it was this sort of bracing which had hitherto helped to keep him tolerably straight. He loved his sister, and 'love," as Jacob Iklunen said, " is the devil's poison ; it is a fire of termr to him, wherein he cannot stay." So, fixing his own clear eyes on the more beautiful dark-blue ones—earnest honest eyes of a very ordinary brown, which always seemed to the lad to iioarch and bring to light all the hidden things that concealed themselves in the dark corner of his con- science till Ray cowered under their inspection, Fielding thundered— ," Coward I 'to revenge your own disgrace on the one who loves.yoti " It is doubtful if the lad understood the -words, but there was something in the voice which he associated with the severely faithful exposure at which he had learnt to wince, of his own morbid' self-conceit, lazi- "tfsss, and self-indulgence. Even Ursula ceased to remonstrate as she also recognised the tone as that of a master, who, young as he was, could, "Read each wound, each weakness cloar, And strike his finger on the place, And say Thou etileet here ana here."

Her cheeks were hot with shame, her eyes dark with a scorn which she could no longer prevent as her brother burst into maudlin tears, and tried to excuse himself in thickened utterance and hiccupping speech. She felt a faintness creep over her -La terror she knew not of what—and though Mrs. Wilson's sympathetic, half-stifled sobs ()Hula be heard from another cornar of the room, she did not feel the slightest inclination to weep. "Oh, what did you say? What does it all mean? —he was never—never like this before !" she cried, as almost a "stound " of agony eame over her, and she tried to remove the hand which covered her besotted face with a nervous grasp that was almost a clutch of the poor slizikin' c, fingers. The knowledge by which her soul seemed to be defiled was coining to her, though she tried to evade it, and tielding—with his dislike to jeopardising her happiness—felb relieved that he would not have to answer her questions. Instead, he stooped down and tried to rearrangethe pillOWs which were shaken by the agitated move- ments of. Raymond's shoulders. ." Let me do it," she said haughtily, in the agony of Ler hicovery, turning on him almost . proudly, and not knowing what she said: "It will be better 'for one of his own flesh and blood to help 'him-than one who must hats and despise him because he is se-,nnfortufiste,7 yielding would not argue with her—he only steed aside and saw the white bawds which had Leen un- soiled by ' any 'mean and tmwortify work, lift the poor head, and Pitt it hack gently on the cushions which they had smoothed. Then he said in a' low , voice. . •

"Do you think that I hate anti despise hint? Would not that be unmanly, a 3 it would be un- womanly." She turned to him again with that dilating of the pupils, making the hazel eyes look almost black, by which she atwaye betrayed the 8 widen pain at her heart, "You say that beeause lam his sister. And yet yen see that now—even now—he is drunk!" He oould not stop the words which were already eat of her lips, but felt—as he bowed his head—like a man who had fired a death shot at a woman, and would give the world to arrest it in its flight, but who knew that the inevitable must take place. "Then," she said, looking at him with her beautiful stormy eyes—the slight hopefulness which had been apparent in her face when he first met her at the station having entirely deserted it—" then you must give him up." "No, not so," he answered in a ringing voice, with which he tried to summon back her failing energy. "He is still worth ten of the other inen who led him into this." "

She looked at him incredulously as he stood ith his arms folded, smiling at her a benevolent encouraging smile. A man in the full swing of his activititm, whom she had once thought ugly, with the flesh wora with those mental efforts which need to be fed with more than their share ..;f the oil of life—a man with one of those faces which convoy less the idea of the number of years passed in this life, than the stored up experiences of a few—a man who had gauged the strength of the foe with which he should have to do battle for this brother's soul. _ _ .

"No; God helping us, we will never give hiinup!" If the real tie which draws kindred spirits to- gether, as strong as that of marriage or blood- relationship, can exist between a man and a woman, then as the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, henceforward to live in a little world of sympathy, were these two souls knit together in a bond of feilowship. He still held apparently aloof. He did not cross the room to help Ursula when she left it with Mrs. Wilson ; but perhaps his look helped her in the wild abandonment; of sorrow which afterwards came upon her. Alone im her lodgings witk the door of her chamber locked, even Fielding would scarcely have recognised the girl lying on the fluor in her desolation —she Whom he had associated with such stateliness and grace. Her ideal palace built upon the sands Was reduced to ruins. The floods had descended upon It, and the rains fell. "God, if Thou (lost exist !" she moaned rather than said, " let Thy curse fall on 2114, but spare my poor brother !" It was the nearest approach to a prayer she yet had uttered, and when we think of the many prayers like dead letters that can never reach Him to whom they are addressed—prayers selfish or egotistical,though full of vain repetitions—let us hope that some ministering angel registered in a merci- ful manner this cry of an unselfish heart. The wild words were painful for her afterwards to remember ; it was difficult for her to reason with herself about them. And yet she said with a little sigh, " I wish I was one of the people who cared for prayers, and believed in the other world—but - I hardly do." The storm had revealed to her the innermost depthsof her ownsoul—depths which she had never before known to exist. fhat ethics were to be as noble in spite of the casting off of old opinions like worn out integuments, not necessary for action,—in spite of the deathfullest denial of divinity in man—had hitherto been a determined assertion of hers. She had trusted "prin erdial to impulses." There had been no space for dreaming of far-off horizons in an energetic life. Prayer seemed to her to be a waste of human energies ratilmal prayer was right action—man's duty to his fellow- men. But she did not yet know herself. Always la soul crises she would turn to it again.
CHAPTER XXIV. A DISAPPEARANCE.

Raymond Campion felt as if hundreds of -hammers were beating on his brain the next morning. Be told himself that he was threatened with delirium— thinking, "Well, if I could be delirious it might be the best thing that could happen," so much did he dread again seeing his sister. He felt his pulse, butdt did not quicken, and yet he was undoubtedly suffer. ing—haring done his best to destroy the temple in which his spirit was located. _

The doctor, who had been called in to see him a few days before, had harped on the wretched state of his nervous system ; and this morning he was more than ever the victim of nerves, every sound excru- ciating him, every footstep making hun start. Fielding' who had been sitting up with him aft night, and had left him to get breakfast, found him on his return sitting upright with a wet towel round his boyish head, altogether a deplorable object. His brow was burning, and he asked for seltzer water, covering His face again with his hands and crying like a child—an exhibition of weakness which ,was not likely to raise him in the opinion of other men.

But Fielding made no remark, and Raymond ap- preciated the delicacy. He was thankful to his friend for refraining from lecturing him, and for sparing his suPerfluons pity. He had a vague idea That he had behaved like a blackguard, not only on the previous night, but on wany other occasions, and he had enough of Ursula in him to hate himself for these escapades.

He began with declaring that he should "spoil" Fielding s "Greats," and then lapsed into praises of his sister. "She was the pick of all the women he knew —ma thousands were mere trumpery, and she was the loyalist and best—he had run through a lot of her money—he was afraid to count up his debts." Still Fielding sat dumb. Not that he would not have done his best to facilitate the "makings clean breast of it," but that experience had taught him how any questioning would be met with evasion, and how difficult it would be to get a full confession of the real truth. , He knew how ready Raymond was always to exonerate himself, and was inclined to say, as he had said more than once before— " Don't look into the small details—the mere mechanism 'of the watch—wind it up and keep it from dust, that is better than fiddling with the works." He was not the lad's tutor now, and was half sorry that he had ever undertaken that tutor- ship. Still when Raymond begged him for Ursula's sake to look at some of his papers and try to get them into a little erder, so that thoy should not worry a girl's eyes, he saw some sense in the request. He would have attempted anythirg that might help to give as harmonious a shape as 'possible to the lad's future for Ursula's sake.

It was disagreeable work, and had to be done rapidly, as they were momentarily expecting the ladies. If Ray had had his usual wits about him he would scarcely have asked for such assistance. And yet he knew that he could hardly fall lower in Field- ing's estimation. The latter tore open envelopes and tossed them into the wastepaper basket. The contents were much of the same sort, threats from duns with whom he had contracted bills long before his name had been entered for the university. They were some of them from Heidelberg, and even from the neighbourhood of Abbeyford, and were accompanied by remonstrating notes from a few of the more patient but still ex- asperated tradesmen. Fielding had to see which of the duns was most savage in his threats. Next he pmeeeded to file the bills, putting down the sums methodically as he did so. "It will not be necessary to enter on the items with Miss Campion •' but I am afraid she will scarcely be able to raise the money at once, out of her usual income, without drawing on some capital," lie thought, practical as usual, and with no time to be bitter.

Then he started at a note which had been left by accident Amongst the tradesmen's letters. It was from one of the men who had been "sent down" —a notorious black sheep—whose fate was to be so quickly followed by Ursula's brother. "Sorry to hear you are having a bad time of it at Oxford. As soon as you leave the cursed hole you can come here for a few days. We can give you a shake-down for a week. Pretty Mrs. Newington, on whom you were such awful spoons when you met her at Abbeyferd, is stopping with my sister. You'll not have such another opportunity as this for a long time. Make hay while the sun shines." Fielding took the letter to Raymond and forced him to look at it. The sensitiveness which at one time had seemed to be almost feminine in the lad's character made him blush like a girl as he seized it and tore it up. Pretty Mrs. Newington had been tabooed in Abbeyford scciety for reasons which need not be detailed. Her mum was notorious, and stunk in the nostrils of men like Fielding. But before a word could be 'said the red colons faded from the cheeks and throat of the young fellow who looked_at him with a sad smile, which, sickly as it was, curved lips as superbly shaped as those of a young Apollo. 'That is only De Travers' chaff. You mustn't throw' me off so far as to believe all that rot about me,' he said, as he Isoked up with an appealing ex- pression in the melancholy violet eyes. Wilfrid Fielding was, as I have said, essentially manly, strong, and self-reliant. Even his gravity had fascinated Ursula Campion, and made her think that if ever she had allowed herself to be seriously-in love —which of course would be too ridiculous and utterly impossible, as if she had tr arried anyone she would have kept herproinise toGrandet —it would have been with a man of such strength of character a.s.Fielding. And yet he was not unsusceptible to the charms of physical beauty. Raymond's horror seemed so real, and the glancs he gave him so ingenuous that his friend never thought!of inquiring whether the sadness in the youth—a sadness from which he sometimes found ! refuge in cards and drink—might be accounted for by some passage in his life which he had kept con- cealed. Ursula, if elm had been a man, might have suspec- ted more of the truth. Fielding contented himself with saying— " You must have nothing more to do with such men as De Travers. Make -up your mind to cut them once and for ever. *ices are habits—habits of weakness--and if a man has no nerve, no root a principle, he is likely enough to fall into such habits." Half-an-hour afterwards, when Ursula came to see him, Ray sat for a time hanging his head, and then a bright thought seemed to strike him, and, with an effort at self-assertion, he said, " It is not exactly a thing to make such a. fuss about! Lots of fellows are sent down, or get much more tipsy than I did, and think nothing of it here." A rich red flamed in her cheeks as she reflected on the meaning of these feeble excuses, and knew that once yielding in Raymond's case might mean always yielding, and that if he could not make an effort to assert his own will, his free agency might desert him. It was useless for her to tell him so. She could not hit a fallen mail ftill less a trother ; but she knew better than Fielding the dangerous passivity which might cause Raymond to be swept away by any social inducements. She bit her lips till the blood came, but she did not argue with him. Instead she looked for help to the friend who was unable to do much for her. Fielding had a sense of satisfaction in her presence which made his blood flow more pleasantly at the very sound of her voice; but at the same he had a conviction of his utter useles.snels in the matter.

"Help me," she said in a low tone; "I am powerless here." But though he looked at her with infinite pity he could only shake his head. "We must have patience," he answered, in an equally low,tone. ' And if a friend, whose voice was as strong as a trumpet to louse others from sloth, • and who had laughed so goodihaturedly at poor Ray's rhapsodies, sympathising with all his enthusiasms, failed to do him any good, what could a woman like herself hope to accomplish? Her heart sank within her. Both looked sadly at each other. Neither of them guessed that help would come from an entirely unexpected quarter. On the evening of the day when the doctor had 'decreed that Raymond might be considered well enough to be moved from Oxford, Fielding came in as usual/10 sit with him, and found to his surprise that the invalid had decamped. The scout was the only person who could throw light on his. absence. The man declared that he had done his best to prevent the imprudent and impulsive youth from exposing himself against medical advice to the night air, but that his entreaties had availed nothing against those of another undergraduate who lodged on the same staircase, and who had decoyed him out. Fielding instantly recognised the name of the undergraduate. It was that of an enthusiast who neglected his work for constant meetings of the Salvation Army, and who had, inundated his fellow students with ' pamphlets and newspapers on the subject. Raymond was just in that feeble state when he *Mild be likely to welcome any new sensation, and I at the barracks of the Salvation Army he would Iprobably be found. Fielding had no difficulty in tracing the headquarters of the Army with large &Unarm letters ever the entrance, wooden sots

CAP'rURE OF SLAVE DHOW. liArmins`e,—A. few days ago some Govern- .. dhows sent etlt to prevent slave trading and the ling of contra:bend gocxls, captured seven dhows to sOuth of 'Trinkitat, after a strong resistance, the and slaves escaping inland. After the capture were found in the dhows incriminating many ..ants with large busin,sses at Jeddah. Three more qrs, loaded with slaves, escaped to sea by fighting `Wav out, several men being wounded in the Go- sent dhows. The captured dhows were brought • condemned by the Government as slavers, and sold. STANLEY EXPEDITION.—EXECUTION OF BARTrELOT'S ASSASSIN. 1110 British East African Company has received a list despatches from their agents. Information has also I to hand from the Stanley Expedition that the Yema porter who shot Major Barttelot has been by court-martial for the murder, and executed is a strong fear now expressed among is portion of officials that TippooTib was more or less privy to assassination of Major Barttelot, as the Manyema ive was quite unknown to the murdered officer, who kever spoken to him. A BONFIRE OF BIBLES. 1.111,13R/D, SUNDAY.—The Liberal Government tries in ' to enforce the spirit of toleration among the ities and subjects' of his Catholic Majesty. Very In Biscay an agent of the Bible Society was Al and insulted by twenty young Catholic students, 4 by a Jesuit father, who excited the lads to take pos- te.ssion of, tear up, and make a pious bonfire of the testaments, and tracts. The Spanish judges, 4iter carefully investigating the case, declined to send the offenders before the tribunals for the assault and destruction of the property of the Bible Society. The Students, and not the Jesuit father, who was the princi- Pal instigator of the outrage, will have to appear before the municipal 'nag's' rate, who can only inflict a fino Ltd a Jew days' arrest even if they are convicted. ..Whilst this treatment is meted out to foreigners and rretestants, Hie Spanish courts of justice send journalists to Penal servitude for criticising State religion. SCENE IN THE FRENCH CHAMBER. A remarkable scene occurred in the French Chamber -4 Deputies on Monday. M. Wilson made Ms first appear- 'lnce since his trial for corrupt practices. Immediately that his presence was observed, a deputy moved the adiournment of the House for the space of one hour by Way of protest, and the motion was -carried. M. Wilson braved it oat until the House reassembled, sad then he Went away.

BOILER EXPLOSION IN RUSSIA.-11 PERSONS KILLED AND 175 INJURED. According to St. Petersburg advices, a terrible boiler ....x:Plosion has just taken place in a large manufactory at Aineshma in Central Russia. 'Eleven persons were killed the spot, while no fewer than one hundred and lty-five persons received serious injuries. AIM

Eviction notices have been served to ten families on the Clanricarde estate, and the relieving officer has been Warned to prepare quarters .inthe workhouse. Ten hounds belonging to the famous Kildare pack were found dead on Monday in the kennels, having been Poisoned by meat which they picked up and ate on the Public road between Kilc ;ck and Naas. while returning from hunting. The Hunt Club have offered a reward of £l.OO for the discovery of the perpetrators of the outrage. There is likely to be another land war in county tionegal. lft is stated that evictions are contemplated on an extensive scale .in the neighbourhood of Falcarra, the priest of- which is the Rev. Father Stevens, who, with the Rev. father M'Fadden, was imprisoned for advo- cating the filati .of Campaign. The potato crop has failed, the people are wretchedly poor, and there is only • very disheartening outlook for the peasantry. Major Purcell O'Gorman, who represented Waterford citybin rarliament up to 1879, died at his residence, Spriogfield, county 'Kilkenny, on Saturday night, after Short illness. The gallant major, whose gigantic figure made him a -remarkable person in the House of Corn- tnone„ wee-in his 70th year. He served in the 90th Light itafantry. and gained some distinction during the Crimean camptagn. On Monday, in the Exchequer Divison, Dublin. judg- ment was given in the Castlereagh conspiracy cases. The questions submitted forthe decision of the Court were— first, whether the defendants were entitled to be fur- nished with a cepv of the depositions at a secret in. quiry ; and, •-econdly, whether legal evidence had been rejected. 'the Court held that the magistrates were right in reusing; the depositions, and on the other point affirmed the conviction.

"THE MANCHESTER MARTYRS." Demonstrations in honour of the " Manchester Martyrs" were announced t o take place in various parts of Ireland on Sunday. In all cases the meetings were Nsclaimed. At Kilkenny. Middleton, Cork, Macknom, New Ross extra police and soldiers were employed to preserve•pence. -11 Nationalist catherine in honour of the "Manchester martyrs" was held in Kilrnali Cemetery on Sunday. Wtaie it was in progress a body of police, armed, en- tered the graveyard: and a Nationalist, named Coete, who declined to be silent at. the bidditir, of an inspector, was dragged from a cross to which he clung. The cemetery was cleared by the police. tiOSECT3TION OF MR. E. BARRINGTON, M.P. At Tralee, on Monday. Mr. Ed. Allarrington, M.P.. was autnmoned under the Crimes Act on three charges of . making specche3, and publishing in the Kerry Sentinel Intimidatory articlu. An application for adjournment be. cause of the Ti inte Commission was refused on the ground that there was no evidence that Mr. Harrington Wita .compulsorily before the Commission, and, as Mr DaTringtoil did not appear, a warrant was issued. MURDER IN KILKENNY. An old •men named Delaney was murdered in his house. O? CastAecomer, county Kilkenny, on Tuesday. Parti- culars of the crime have not been received, and the Daotive is unknown. A later telegram says the murder was due to a family dispute. Delaney, who was 80 veers old, hearing a quar- rel between his niece an.; hr buThand, Dan Mo.Evoy, With whom he lived, tried to make peace, hut Mc.Evoy, resenting his interference, struck him on the head with aspade, killing him on the spot. Mc.Evoy surrendered himself to the police, and has been lodged in Kilkenny gaol.

The Irish 'Parnell Indemnity Fund new amounts to £20,000. Sir Henry Blake rolled on the Colonial Secretary on Monday, and was informed that his formal resignation of the Governorship of Queensland Rad boten accepted. FATHER M'FADDEN IN LIVERPOOL. Father Wradden addressed a large gathering of Irish- men in Liverpool on Sunday. it had been reported that. g Papa I prohibition was to be issued preventing his attendance at this and other meetings in England, and considerable interest was attached to Father M'Fadden's appearance. He said he had been dealt with unfairly by Lord Claude John Hamilton, who had expressed a hope that Rome would interfere to prevent him addressing audiences in England; but the Hamiltons were the last People in the world he shoukl expect to find seeking assistance from Rome. The fact was, though the Pro- testants of Gweedore were but a handful, be had fought for them as well as the Roman Ottholics. Referring to the Land Purchase Bill now in the nouse of Commons, be challenged Lord Claude Hamilton to deny that the nonillion family would benefit to the tune of £238,000 by the bill. The Hamilton family had a direct interest, In the bill passing through Farliament. The bill was an injustice to the Irish people and the British taxpayers. Fie had served six months' imprisonment, and his (Father 111'Fadden's) spirit was not broken yet. MR. PARNELL'S ACTION AGAINST 7HE 'TIMES. Mr. Parnell's action for £50,000 damages against The. Times for libel came before the First Division Court of Ses- sion, Edinburgh, on Saturday, on a reclaiming note from Lord Kinnear's judgment allowing proof on the question of arrestrnents. Mr. Grailitrn Murray addressed the court for the reclaimers and defenders, and their lord- ships, without calling on the other side, delivered judg- ment. —The Lord President said he entirely agreed with Lord Kinnear in allowing proof as to arrestments It would indeed be rash to say that on the face on the record there was no good arrestment to found jurisdic• , tion on. The averments that such arrestments had been made were irrelevant. They did not appear irrelevant. and if the averments were established the arrestments would probably be found good. The other judges con- curred, and the case was sent to Lord Kinnear for proof TFIE 'HOLBORN CONTEST: THE NOMINATIONS. The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the represents cf the Holb,,rn Division of Finsbury, caused by the death of Col. Duncan, was fixed to take place at Holborn Town Da, between the hours of 11 and one on Monday. The nomination papers of Mr. Gainsford Bruce (Conservative) and Earl Compton (Gladstonian Liberal) were tendered, but the returning officer refused to accept that of Earl Compton. No fresh nonination papers had been handed in at noon. It appeared that there was some informality in Earl , Compton'a nomination paper, the candidate being described simply as Earl Compton, instead of his fun title—the Right Hon, William George Spencer Scott, commonly called Earl Compton. At 12 40, Earl Comp- ton returned to the place of nomination, followed by his 'Tent, and an amended paper was submitted to and accepted by the returning officer. Both candidates were then &eared dilly nominated

TIOUSE OF COMMONS,—MoNnar. The Sneaker took the chair at 3 5 mm. Amidst laughter, Mr, ByaoN REED inquired whether the Chancellor of the Exchequer was prepared to tax wall posters, to which Mr. GOSCHEN replied that the difficulty he had experienced in persuading the public to accept new taxes was so great that he was not en- eouraged to propose a fresh one, although he wee nt prepared to say there were not arguments in favour ot taxation in the direction indicated. Mr. MACLURE asked the Chancellor of ,the Exchequer whether he could give an estimate of the amount which would be produced by the Van and Wheel Tax in Ene,- ;end,and also state how much would be received by the various county boroughs, and how much by ench of the separate counties independently of the county boroughs. —The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said he esti- mated the amount at £lBO,OOO. He was unable to say with accuracy how that amount would be distributed. ;Alt generally he thought it would be—to London .C 37,000 to the county boroughs £60,000, and to the rest at England and Wales £82,600. Sir J. FERGUSSON, in reply to Mr. Picten, said the Sugar Bounties Convention had no binding effect what- ever without ratification. In the present case legislm 'ion would be necessary in order to give effect to the Convention, and therefore when a measure was sub- mitted to Parliament for that purpose an opportunity would be afforded for discussion. IRISH LAND PURCHASE. Mr. W. H. Swett moved the suspension of the Stand- .tig Orders relating to the 12 o'clock rule, and on a divi- don being taken, it was carried by a majority of 72, 207 voting for and 135 voting against the motion. The House then went into Committee on the Land Purchase Bill.—Mr. PARNELL moved the addition of a proviso that no advance shall be made for the purchase of more than one holding in the occupation of any one tenant if such holding be of the ratable value of not less than £2O a year, the main abject of the amendment 'wing to prevent advances being made to nonresident and pluralist tenents.—Mr. Sexton, Mr. T. Healy, Mr. Murphy, Mr. W. O'Brien, Mr. Gill, Mr. P f. Power, Mr. Sheehy, and other members advocated the amendment; but Mr. A. S. BALFOUR opposed it on the ground that it would exclude many of the most deserving tenants from the benefits of the Act.--Sir IV. HARCOVRT.. who read an advertisement of land to let with the stipulation that none but Protestants need apply," maintained that the amendment was required so prevent the establishment of Protestant plantatioee. —Mr. T. W. RUSSELL oontended that the amendment would have the effect of preventing fictitious tenants. —After a few remarks from Mr. Labouchere, the ; debate was interrupted.
BREACH OF PRIVILEGE. SCENE.-SELECT COMMITTEE APPOINTED.

Mr. SHEEHY moved to report progress for the purpose of complaining that he had been served in the lobby ot the House with a summons under the Coercion Act.— Mr. BRADLA.46II seconded the motion. Mr. Ilaimonv : I thoroughly endorse what has been said by the hon. member. (Loud Opposition cheers.) 1 do not in the least know who is to blame for this, whether it is the Chief Secretary for Ireland or whoever it may be, but I say publicly it is a scandal. (Renewed cheers.) Mr. A.. 5. BALVOIIR, amid much excitement, admitted that is WAS a grievous and unhappy thing, but he dis- claimed any knowledge of or responsibility for what had happened, and gave an assurance that if it rested with the Executive such an occurrence should not occur again. Sir W. Haricot:lnt. explained that one of the ordinary cards used by visitors had been sent into the House to Mr. Sheehy, having upon it the name of a member of the Royal Irish Constabulary. He ridiculed the notion that the Executive were not responsible, and he urged that progress should be reported in order that toe cir- cumstances might be dealt with with the Speaker in the

chair. Mr. W. H. SMITH consented to progress being re- ported, and on the Speaker taking the chair he moved the appointment of a Select Committee to consider the matter. He stated, in answer to questions from the Liberal benches, that the Committee would sit to- morrow, to which Mr. SEXTON took objection, insisting that the Committee should sit " forthwith," and he asked for a pledge that further summonses should not be served upon Irish members within the precincts of the House. Mr. COURTNEY also advocated the sitting of the Com- mittee forthwith. After some further discussion, a Committee was ap- pointed, consisting of Mr. Matthews, Mr. Childers, Mr. Goschen, Sir C. Russell, Mr. J. Morley, the Solicitor- General, the Solicitor-General for Ireland. Mr. Parnell, Sir M. White-Ridley, Mr. Hanbury, and Mr. 'T. Healy, and it was ordered to sit forthwith. Mr. W. H. SMITH then proposed to proceed with the Committee on the Purchase Bill, but objection was taken to this, and ultimately it was agreed to suspend the sitting until 10 o'clock. When the sitting was resumed it was reported that the Select Committee had adjourned till Thursday, pend- ing the arrival of witnesses from Ireland. THE LAND PURCHASE BILL. On the Committee resuming the consideration of the ,and Purchase Bill a division was taken on Mr. Par- nail's amendment, wkich was negatived by 154 to 111. A ,proviso moved by Mr. PICTON, that the Commis- bioners shall give preference to estates valued at not more than £l,OOO, was withdrawn after seine discussion in favour of an amendment moved by Mr. SEXTON, giving the Commissioners a discretion as to the estates they should allow to be purchased under the Art; but this was opposed by Mr. A. J. BALFOUR and rejected on a,division by 180 to 118.—A division was also taken on the question that the clause stand part of the bill. and it was carried by 177 to 111. Mr. J. MORLEY moved a new clause providing for quarterly returns showing the working of the Aot.—Mr. BALFOUR objected, but was willing to grant the returns if moved for in the usual way.—After discussion, Mr. BALPOUR moved the closure, which was carried on a division by 174 to I.); and a division being also taken on the clause, it was rejected by 166 to 108, after which the Committee adjourrnsl. The House adjourned at 2 25 a.m.

The 'House went int" Committee On the Oaths Bill. Several amendments affecting, the scope and principle of the hill were discussed, but ultimately withdrawn in order not to imperil the hill passing into law. The LORD CHANCELLOR pressed a new clause giving the right to challenge a juror declaring that he had no religious belief to a division, and his amendment was defeated by 14 tot The bill passed through Committee without amend- ment. Several bills were advanced a stage, and the Douse adjourned.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Timener. QUESTIONS. Mr. Rirmira promised to make inquiry respecting some alleged disastrous results arising from vaccination, the details of which were recorded in questions standing on the paper in the name of Mr. Picton. Mr. W. IT. Smrrn, replying to Mr. J. Stevenson and Mr Howard Vincent, said he regretted he could not yet say when the discussion on the second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday Bill, or proceeding with the Patents, Designs, and Trade Marks Bill would take place. _ _ . .

, The Homa SECRETARY said the new Commissioner of Police was not yet appointed. The LORD ADVOCATE said attention had been given to corrupt practices in municipal elections in Scotland, but he could not promise a bill on the subject. BRITISH TROOPS TO ASSIST THE EGYPTIAN FORCES.

Mr. W. U. Smrru, replying to Mr. J. Morley, said com. munications between her Majesty's Government and the Egyptian Government had taken place, and the offer ot assistance of British troops had been accepted by the latter Government. The operations of the British troops would be confined to the immediate neighbour- hood of Suakim,

div.head: IRISH LAND PURCHASE BILL.
div.p: THE IRISH LAND PURCHASE BILL.

The House went into Committee on the Irish Land l'urchase Bill.—Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRIC moved a new elause limiting advances. The object of his clause would be to limit the operation of the Act to tenancies of about £lOO per annum. If they went beyond that they would depart from the ostensible object of the Act The new clause was as follows—" No advance should be made by the Land Commissioners to any one tenant purchaser. in respect of any application made after the passing of the Act exceeding the sum of £2.000 in all. —Mr. A. I. Ilkixotra opposed. The proposal had already been discussed by anticipation. If large hold- ings were excluded from the benefit of this great reme- dial measure, they would become centres of disaffection. —Mr. SR/CTON supported the clause. He believed purchasing a few holdings would prevent the purchase of a great many small ones.—Mr. FL H. Fowtsa sup- ported the clause. Lord 11. CHURCHILL could not admit it was ever in- tended that the Ashbourne Act should apply only to the smaller class of tenants. It would be very injurious if the sale of large estates, embracing a larger number of small tenancies, was prevented from being carried ot,t because there might be a single tenant of £5OO per annum. _

Mr. Rathbone, Dr. Clark, Sir J. Campbell, and Mr. Childers supported the clause. Mr. T. HEALY said if the Government would depart from their determination to accept no amendment to the bill, and accept the proposed clause, they would facilitate the bill through Committee. Mr. A. BALFOUR said he could not accept the proposal as it stood. He should have no objection to a dame

to the effect that an advaitee should be mane by the Irish Land Commissiontrs nyder she Lane Law (irelan Bill exceeding the sum of ,83,000, except in the opinion of the Land Commissioners IV! AdVETIOC of such a :arger sum, not exceeding £5,00', be expedient far carrying ont the sale of a whole estate—After a Short discussion the proposed new clause was withdrawn. Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE then moved a new clause, provid7 inn' that no advances should be made to tenants whi had not occupied their tenaney for five veers. This :dense was directed agailut bogus tenaneles being mans- iactured.—Mr. A. IgAI.FOtTrt opposed. He did net be- lieve in the existence of the abuse against whioh the clause was directed.—A long discussion ensued, several Irish members contending that bogus tenants were minufactured by Irish landlords.—The &awe Vi as rejected by IEO to 93. A new clause dealing with the limitation of advances was agreed to in the farm which had been suggested by Mr. A. RALFOI`R, and added to the bill. Mr. T. Fiesix moved a new cla.ise, providing that the approval of the Commissioners to sanotsen any advanos should be signified by an order as to tile date on whiarit such approval was made, and after such date the vendee should be discharged from all liabilities affecting the holding, includin, all rent and arrears.—After a Short discussion the clause was agreod to. Mr. T. Hasty moved a new Cause. providing that two additional Land Commissioners, appointed under the Act of 1835, should hold their offices for seven years after the passing of this A cl,.—The SOLIGITOR-fFENERAL for iwirtaign objected to dealing with that matter in the present bill—After a discussion, T. HEALY withdrew his proposal, intimating he would move it on report Mr. T. FIF.ALT mimed a new clause, providing that the Commissioners should make no advance to a tenant pending, proceedings wit the pert of the landiord.—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IHIMAND contended that suffi- cient protection wits already afforded the tenant. —Mr. IL 11. FOWLER thought the Commissioners ought to be forbidden to comirin any contract entered into under duresa—Ultimately the clastse was rejeeted by 205 tat 142. Mr. HEALY then moved a new clause providing that no money should he advanced to any person in receipt of salary paid out of taxes without a speeial report be- ing made on the subject to Parliament.—Mr. BALFOUR did not think that the hon. gentleman seriously meant this clause, which, although directed against the Lord Lieutenant, would Include the humblest Government official in Ireland.—The dense was negatived without a division. Mr. Hastr next moved another new Meuse, requiring notice of intended purchase, so that a person might ap- pear against granting an advance.—The Someone- GENSCRAL for IRELAND ObleCtred te the elause as giving no protection to either landlord or tenant, and as causing unnecessary delay. Mr. O'Donsitrir, who spoke with great animation, created loud laughter by sitting down on his hat. The committee divided on the proposed new dense— For the clause, 97; against, 165; majority against, 68. Mr. T. P. O'CoNnott moved te report progress. (Oh, oh.)—After a heated altercation, the motion for re- porting progress was withdrawn. The other amend- ments on the paper were withdrawn, and the bill, as amended, was reported to the House. The other orders of the day having been gone through, the House adjourned at 2 40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Winmesn,ty. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock. Quesrioxs.—Mr. W. H. Sutra said it was true that Mr. Mutton had been appointed chief commissioner of the metropolitan police. Mr. CIINNINGRAMB GRAMIX had earlier asked, amid laughter, whether Sir H. BLAKE, the proposed governor of Queensland, had received the post, to which Mr. W. H. SMITH replied hat the sugges- tion was an utter absurdity. Replying to Mr. SEXTON, the Chief Secretary for Ireland said the warrant against Mr. E. HARRINGTON would not be enferced in such manner or time as would prevent him from attending the House while the Irish Estimates were under dicua- Bien. flume LAND Bitb.—Tite consideration of the Land Purchase Bill was then resumed, and a number of amendments were dealt with. Mr. W. H. Sterns announced certain concessions which the Government were prepared to make, and asked, in return, that the discussion should be shortened. The third reading of the bill was fixed for next day. THE VAN AND WHIRL Tax.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, in reply to a friendly question put by Sir MARRON BORTH- wicx, announced, amid laughter and ironical cheering, the withdrawal of the Wheel and Van Tax Bill. The remaining orders disposed of, the House adjourned at six o'cloek. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—.TIEURSDAY.

The pumps were immediately brought into operation, but the flames were not got under until much of the cargo had beeF destroyed by the fire and water. The damage is esti- mated at £2,000.

DESTRUCTIVE FlRE.—About no en Monday, destruetive fire was discovered by the watchtnan Oetram's mill, Greetland, near Halifax. A two-storyed buildlng ured for drying and pressing pieces WES com- pletely gutted. Owing to the dry state of the material,' the flames spread very rapidly. Two hundred men are thrown out of employment. The damage will probably reach £5,000. The two men whe have confessed to the Edlingbare burglary, for which two innocent persons were in 1879 sent to penal servitude for life, were brought before Baron Pollock on Saturday, at Newcastle Assizes. Petition', bearing 3,000 names, craving mitigation of punistnnent. were presented. Sentences of five years' penal servitude were passed. The innocent men, whose cane has been mentioned in Parliament, are now cut on license. Replyine to a large deputation of employes of the London and North-Western Railway Co.. on Monday. the Horne Secretary said he was satisfied that if em- ployers behaved as this company had done, the result would be more beneficial to the men than any system et enforced liability, and it was in order not to destroy such arrangements that he introduced an insurance, Meuse into the Employers' Liability Bill. So far as he had any influence, he would stand by that clause. An inquest was held at Manchester, on Monday, on the body of William Morris Pugh, landed proprietor, et Liverpool. who committed suicide in the Spread Eagle Hotel, on Saturday. He was supplied with brandy an soda that morning, but was not asetin seen alive. His door being forced ripen he was found dead, shot through the right terniale. Letters found stated that suicide wa, the result of lieigation with his brother. A verdiet e Suicide whilst insane" was returned. The schools have beer, ender the control of the Mariboroueh family for a long period. There has been some differences between thr Puke of Marlborough and the Rev. A. Majendie, recto -4 Woodstock, the latter having declined to have th- church bells rung when his Grace brought his wife holm recently from New York.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. Qunsnows.--Questionecl by Mr. Dillon about British, operations at Suakin', Mr. SMITH said nothing was being kept back on this subject. No serious or import- ant movement was contemplated on the part of her Majesty's Goverment. Mr. Surrn said he did not think he was called upon to take any action in the case of Mr. Gent-Davis, whereupon Mr. T. HEALY said that, unless action were taken by the Government in the meantime, he should on Tuesday next move that the Speaker issue his writ for a new election for Kennington. CONTEMPT OF Couny.—Mr. Bradlaugh moved the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to the protracted imprisonment of Thomas Moroney for " contempt " in refusing to answer questions in the Irish I Bankruptcy Court in reference to the Plan of Campaign.' He said Moroney had already had twenty-three times the amount of punishment which could be inflicted upon him under the Coercion Act even for refusing to answer questions in a murder case, and his mental health was now breaking down, and that to the knowledge of the Irish Secretary and Solicitor General. Dr. Kenny seconded the motion, and testified from personal knowledge to Moroney's weak condition. Mr. BALEous said it was in Moroney's power at any moment to purge his contempt by taking the oath. After a long debate the House divided, when there voted—for the adjonroment, 159 ; against, 195; majority for the Government, 36. Tint hum LAND BILL.-011 the motion for the third reading of the Irish Land Purchase Bill Dr. CLAIM moved the rejection of the measure. The division resulted in the third reading being carried by 202 votes to 141. The Excise Duties (Local Purchases) Bill was withdrawn, and two other bills having been advanced a stage, the House adjourned at 12 2.

AN INCAUTIOUS RAILWAY PBSSENGER KILLED.—Lit 4, m Saturday night a young man, named John Gaunt, e! stanningley, near Bradford, met with a terrible death ..n the railway at Haddon. He was leaning with half hi,- nody out of a carriage window talking to two girls ir the next compartment whilst the train was proceedint>, when his head came in contact with the side of a tunnel Fits body was jerked out of the carriage on the tine, anc tie was instantaneously kilted. Be was 21 years of agr, and was the nephew of an ex-Mayor of Leeds.

SHOCKING SUICIDE 7N AN ITOTF.L.—A determined nen premeditated case ef suicide was discovered in tte Spread Eagle Hotel, Manchester. on Saturday night. inan giving the name of Morris, who is said to have ha., strange manner, had been staying in the hotel for ever s week. On Saturday morning he was supplied will ,•ortie refreshment, and nothing more seen of him utrti flight, when his bedroom door was forced open, and he wa found dead, sitting in an armchair. He had stripped him wit and put on his nightdress, and then shot himself ir, die right, temple with a revolver, which he still held in ids right hand when found dead. He had written s letter to his brother asking that his wife might be in. formed of the event, thus showing the deed was pre- meditated. His real name was found from the letter to, be William Morris Pugh. ' A GAMEKEEPER SWOT DEAD DT A FOACHER.—A part) of keepers were out on Saturday night watching in the neighbourhood of Leith Hill, Dorking, a district that abounds with preserves. Between three and four o'clock on Sunday morning a number of shots were fired, aria. going in tin direction from which the reports came, the keepers came rpm two men in a cover ution the estate of Mr. Steere (formerly member for East Surrey) st Ockley. The men were taken by surprise, and one e; them, a navvy named Edwards, was seized. He offered 'ittle resistance, but his companion ran away. He was a once followed by a keeper named Groombridge. Be had not run far when the poacher turned, and, takins deliberate aim, fired at the keeper, who received the con tents of the gun in his breast, and fell mortally wounded .01110 of the other keepers rushed to his assistance, but iie expired almost immediately. The murderer mean while made his escape. A man, supposed to be the mut ,terer, was afterwards arrested. A. RELIGIOUS CENSUS OF ROCHDALE. —ln accord- -trice with a resolution of the Rochdale Town Coon a religious census of the parish of Rochdale has ' recently been taken. The resolution directed that it b,. ,seertained what is "the number of places of public worship of God, the number of sittings provided therein and also the number of Sunday schools and scholars with ir the district of the Poor-law Union of Rochdale: the re- turn to also state the name of the sect to which each oisilding belongs." The return shows that the sittimgs in the Church of England churches are 25,09, its agains, ,63.40 sittings in the Nonconformist Churches. The num tier of teachers and scholars in the Church of Englane ,unday Schools is 17,987, as against 34,652 scholars am. teachers in the Noncorrformist Sunday Schools. Th! object with which the return was moved for was ti show that the Ecclesiastical Commissioners were no. eistified in taking the funds derived from the gleb, lands to provide Church accommodation for which then was no demand in the parish. TERRIBLE HOUSE FIRE A WHOLE FAMILY LOST.-- A calamitous fire, by which five persons lost theiT lives, occurred about four a.m. on Monday' in a small and poor thoroughfare, known as the High Woods. in the rural parish of Mlle End, Colchester. William Holland, a plasterer, lived there in a small cottage witi: his wife and three children, his next-door neighbout being James Cole. The tatter was aroused abow three o'clock by the barking of s dog, Mu' found his house full of smoke. He went down stairs, and discovered Holland's house ablaze. He oh tamed the assistance of a neighbour, named Nicholl, anc broke open the door of Holland's house. They fount' Mrs. Holland lying on the floor, enveloped in flames. am' Nichol' was unable to reach her. Holland himself anc: his three children were lying at the bottom of ttu staircase dead,' and his wife was burned to death, before the eyes of her would -be rescuers. It is supposed that Holland was endeavouring to folloe his wife downstairs to the front door, with the children. and that he and they were overcome by the flames, am' suffocated. Holland was 34 years of age, and his wift two years older. The fire brigade from Colchester was summoned, but the water supply was scanty, and tie flames spread, resulting in the destruction of three out of six cottages. The other inhabitants escaped. The origin of the conflagration is unknown. Holland was an eccentric man, and it is rumoured that he set fire to the house. On Thursday last, Mrs. Holland received a letter from her husband, dated from Waltham. stow, where he was then at work, hinting at self- destruction. He returned home en Saturday night. 11, was a man of temperate habits. The children were in bed at the time of the fire, and the bedsteads containing them fell through the floor into the burning,room below.
