TILE EXAMINER, SATISRDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1888. ;RAL • NEWS. A SUICIDAL MANIA AT WARRINGTON.

During the last few days Warrington has boon shocked by the news of the suicide of a well-known tradesman, followed by the attemp- ted suicide of his son, and by the particulars of an attempt at suicide by a boy. A report of the circumstances attending the death of Mr. Winstanley, who committed suicide last even- ing week, appeared in last Saturday's issue of the "Examiner." On Saturday a boy named Thomas smith, who is only fourteen years of age, cut his throat with his father's rasor, and on Monday Joseph Winstanley, a son of the late Joseph Winstanley, jumped into the canal at Latchford, but was fortunately rescued. THE SUICIDE OF A TRADESMAN. On Monday evening Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-west Lancashire, attended at the Marquis of Granby Inn, Church-st., Warrington, to inquire into the circumstances of the death of Joseph Winstanley (66) provisioa dealer and reed maker, 62 Church-st., when various witnesses were called to give evidence.—Emma Winstanley, daughter of the deceased,said that her father had been ill for along I time, and latterly he had not got up from bed until four or five o'clock in the afternoon. On the Friday previous he came downstairs at about that time, and laid down on the sofa. Presently he went into the back-yard of the house. Shortly afterwards someone came to the door and said—" There's a man in the well, with red slippers on; have you missed anyone." Witness went out, saying "It is I my father.' The deceased was lying with his back on the nags, his head and shoulder being in the I well. Ile was dead. With assistance witness lifted , him away. A bit of string was round his wrists, and his arms were behind him. Witness cut the string. Her father had been in a low, despondent sort of way for some time. He had never in her ! presence said that he would take away his life, and she never suspected that he would, but she had aoticed that he was strange in his manner. Ile ' had been under the care of Dr. White.—Margaret Inglis, wife of William Inglis, 58 Church-street, next door to where deceased lived, said that at aboust half-past five o'clock on the Friday afternoon in question she told her daughter Maggie to fetch some water, and she went to the back of the house for that purpose. The next moment she shouted "Oh, Ma, there's a man lying in the back-yard." Witness thought her daughter was in danger, and called out for help. Some of the neighbours came up, and the body of the deceased was then found as ! described by the previous witness.—Margaret Inglis (11), gave corroborative evidence.—Horatio Slack, engine fitter, 60 Church-st., also deposed to being I present when the body was found. Deceased, he added, had suffered a great deal, and at times had not been in his right mind, lie looked strange.— Dr. White, who had attended the deceased, said that !he (deceased) had been suffering from an affection of the brain for the last two years. Ile had had a kind of stroke, from which he had never recovered, and his mind had been going ever since. The ! deceased had a curious perversion of sensation--if he felt anything cold it gave him the sensation !of extreme heat, and vies versa. Witness did not ' look upon him as a sane man.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst insane.--A juror remarked that the well was rather of a dangerous character, and pointed out that if it happened to be left uncovered a child might accidently fall in and be drowned.— The jury thereupon added the following present- ment to the verdict—" The jury present that the lid of the cistern should be reconstructed, as in its present state the cistern is unprotected and danger- ous to life." TIIE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT LATCHFORD. At the Borough Police Court,on Tuesday morning, Joseph Winstanley (33), of 62, Church-st., a wire- drawer employed at the works of Messrs. Rylands, was brought up in custody on a charge of having attempted to commit suicide by jumping into the Latchford and Runcorn Canal, near Black Bear Bridge, Latchford, on the morning of the previous day. He pleaded guilty. In narrating the circum- stances to the Bench, Mr. Hunt, the chief constable, said that the defendant was in a bad state of health, and had been seriously ill at the beginning of the year. He had gone through serious trouble recently and that, together, perhaps, with a little drink, had led up to what had occurred. On the morning pre- vious he was seen by a man named George Adams, on the canal bank, with a piece of string round his hands. He seemed to be trying to put his feet through some string. Adams then saw him jump backwards into the canal, and, as he could not swim, he ran to fetch a pole. In the meantime a man named Peter Cliff, a porter in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, who had also seen what had occurred, ran to the spot and jumped into the water to the assistance of the defendant. Adams helped Cliff, and the two with great difficulty got the defendant out of the water. Defendant was taken to the police station, and when charged he said—" I did not know what I was doing."--Defendant; I did not know what I was doing.—Mr. White: (Magistrates' Clerk) : Have you any promises to make about the future. —Defendant: 1 will promise to be a steady man.— Mr. R. Garnett (who presided on the Bench) asked the defendant if lie bad not been steady lately.— Defendant said that he had held his present employ- ment for eighteen years, but latterly he did not think that the work agreed with him. He had not I been a teetotaler, but he had been steady.—Mr. Hunt said that the police had never heard anything lagainst the defendant.—Mr. Garnett said the magis- trates were very sorry to see the defendant in that position. Ile would have to find two sureties, in .£lO, for his good behaviour. The Bench felt very much indebted to Cliff and Adams for the part they had taken in the matter. They had done a good service to a brother—saved his life and perhaps saved something more.—On the conclusion of the business of the Court the Bench directed that Cliff and Adams should each receive the sum of 10s. as an acknowledgment of their services. It may be added that this is the second time that Cliff has been instrumental in saving life. About fourteen years ago he rescued a man named Mullen from the canal at Moore, and on that occasion was so exhausted by his efforts that he was for some time unconscious. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A BOY. A determined attempt at suicide was made on Saturday night by Thomas Smith, a lad PI years of age, who lives with his parents at 20 Allen-street, Warrington. Ills father, Simeon Smith, is a barman employed at the Rodney Vaults, Town's-end. Shortly before 10 o'clock on Saturday evening, the boy was sent to bed with two younger brothers, his mother afterwards going out on business. On returning at midnight with her husband they found to their horror bloodmarks on the slopstone in the scullery, the back door being open, and on going through into the yard they found their son lying unconscious on the ground with his throat cut almost from ear to ear. Medical aid was at once summoned, and Dr. Sherratt, who was quickly in attendance, ordered the lad's removal to the Infirmary, where he now lies under the care of the house surgeons. So far as can be gathered the youth left his bed when he heard his mother go out, and, abstracting from a drawer in the dressing table his father's razor, lie inflicted two severe woundg in his throat, one on either side, but fortunately did not touch the windpipe. From his bedroom, the bloodstains show, he made his way into a back room, and afterwards downstairs into the scullery, and finally to the yard where he was found. We understand that the lad has been for years addicted to sleep-walking, and as he went to bed in apparently good spirits this circumstance may throw some light upon his strange conduct. SUICIDE OF A WARRINGTON GOVERNESS. The body of Miss Longshaw, a Warrington lady, who had been missing since the previous Wednes- day, was on Saturday discovered in the river Vyrnwy. For the past four years she had been engaged as governess to Mr. Moon, of Llanymynech, near Oswestry. She had been in a desponding state of mind for some time, and on Wednesday last left the house suddenly at night. Search was made for her throughout the neighbourhood, but without success until Saturday, when her body was found in the river. At the inquest, which was held at Llanymynech, near Oswestry, on Monday night, the jury returned a verdict that deceased drowned herself whilst temporarily insane, no motive being assigned.

div.head: TRIPLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: TRIPLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.

About six o'clock on Monday morning, a points- man. named James Jervis, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Co.,at Betley,Staffordshire, murdered his wile and two children, and afterwards committed suicide. It appears that the wife of Jervis was seen by her neighbours to rush from the house. Some men who were passing entered, and found the two children lying dead with their throats cut. Another child was found with a cut on the face, but the wound was not serious. Jervis himself lay on the ground, also with his throat cut, but he was alive His wife, who had been similarly treated, ran into a neighbour's house, and there fell and died from loss of blood. Medical assistance was sent for, and Jervis's injuries attended to, but he soon expired. When founa ho was grasping a large table-knife in his right hand, whilst another knife was sticking in his throat. Jervis was living on friendly terms with his wife, by whom he had had it children.

The inquiry into the circumstances attending tne tragedy was held on Wednesday by Mr. J. Booth, county coroner. The jury found that Mrs. Jervis and the two children were murdered by James Jervis, the head of the household, and that Jervis committed suicide whilst of unsound mind.

div.head: TIIE SELECT •COMMITTEE AND MR,
div.p: TIIE SELECT •COMMITTEE AND MR,
SIIEEILY, M.P.

The Select Committee appointed to inquire into the circumstanoes connected with the attempt- to serve a summons on Mr. David Sherthy,, M.P., in the central lobby of the House of Commons, Met on Monday in Mr. Gladstone's room, and appointed Mr. Matthews chair- man. Mr. Sheehy was called, and asked to give his ver- sion of the circumstances. He said he had spoken in the debate in Committee on the Land Purchase Bill, and was going from the House to the dining-room, when a visitor's ticket wos handed to him, on which was the name "Jeremiah Sullivan, Limerick?' Mr. Sheehy said that he did not Rotice at the time that the letters "It I. C." were written in the corner. He went into the central lobby, where he saw Sullivan. whom he recognised at once as a policeman in plain clothes. He said: "What do you want with me ?" Sullivan replied: "Perhaps you don't know that I have a summons for you," and he invited Mr. Sheehy to step aside. Mr. Sheehy declined to do so, and called the attention of the officer on duty to the man's conduct. Mr. Sheehy wa,k invited by the committee to retire, and then the officer Sullivan was asked to give his explanation. After hear- ing Sullivan's evidence the committee recalled Mr. Sheehy, and questioned him as to whether the officer's words were not "Come outside," instead of "Stet. aside." Mr. Sheehy assured them that the words" Step aside" were used, because when he asked, "Don't von know of the privileges of the House of Commons?" Sul- livan replied, "But this is not 'aside the House." Th, committee adiourned until Thursday.

• The Select Committee of the House of Commons on the privilege question of Monday last held another sitting on Thursday, and took further evidence as to the instructions given to Sergeant Jeremiah Sullivan on his being told off to serve summonses on Irish members of Parliament in London.

SCENES AND INCIDENTS ON BOARD A CUNARDER FROM LIVERPOOL TO NEW YORK. Of all the great Atlantic steamship lines the Cunard still stands without a rival in popularity. Its steamers are not only the fastest, hut excel all in comfort and general attendance. Life on board one of these floating palaces is not, as some may suppose, one of dull routine, but full of inci- dents; acquaintances are quickly made, friendships are established of which many interesting tales are told in after years. I late United States Consul at one of the English ports relates the following:— "On my last voyage from England, on one of the Cunard steamers, I noticed one morning, after a few days out of port, a young man hobbling about on the upper deck, supported by crutches and seeming to move with extreme difficulty and no little pain. He was well dressed and of exceedingly handsome countenance, but his limbo were emaciated and his face sallow, which bore traces of long suffering. As he seemed to have no attendant or companion, he at once attracted my sym- pathies, and I went up to him as he leaned against the taffrail looking out on the foaming track which the Steamer was making. 'Excuse me, my young friend,' I said, touching him gently on the shoulder, 'you appear to be hardly able or strong enough to trust yourself unattended on an ocean voyage, but if you require any ' assistance I shall be glad to help you.' 'You are very kind,' he replied, in a weak voice, 'but I require no present aid beyond my crutches, which enable me to pass from my stateroom up here to get the benefit of the sunshine and the tea breeze.' 'You have been a great sufferer, no doubt,' I said, 'and I judge that you have been afflicted with rheumatism, whose prevalence and intensity teem to be on an alarming increase both in England and America.' 'You are righ,' 'he answered; I have been its victim for two years, and after failing to find relief from medical skill, have lately tried the springs of Carlsbad and Vichy: but they have done me no good, and lam now on my return home to Missouri to die, I ' suppose. I shall be content if life is spared me to reach my mother's presence. She is a widow, and lam her only child. There was a pathos in this speech which affected me profoundly, and awakened in me a deeper sympathy than I had felt before. I had no words to answer him, and stood silently besides him, watching the snowy wake of the ship. While thus standing, my thoughts reverted to a child—a ten-year old boy—of a neighbour of mine residing near my consulate residence, who had been cured of a stubborn case of rheumatism by the use of St Jacobs Oil, and I remembered the steward of the ship had told me the day before that he had cured himself of a very severe attack of the gout in New York, just before his las, voyage, by the use of the remedy. I at once left my young friend and went below to find the steward. I not only found him off duty, but dis- covered that he had a bottle of the Oil in his locker, which he had carried across the ocean in case of another attack.' lie readily parted with it on my representation, and, hurrying up again, I soon persuaded the young man to allow me to take him to his berth and apply the remedy. After doing so, Icovered him up snugly in bed, and requested him not to get up until I should see him again. That evening! returned to his state-room, and ' found him sleeping peacefully and breathing gently. I roused him, and inquired how he felt. Like a new man,' he answered, with a grateful smile. 'I feel no pain, and am able to stretch my limbs without difficulty. I think I'll get up.' 'No, don't get up to-night,' I said, but let me rub yon again with the Oil, and in tte morning you will be much better able to go above.' I then applied the Oil, again rubbing his knees, ankles, and arms thoroughly, until he said he felt as if lie had a mustard poultice all over his body. I then left him. The next morning when I went up on deck, I found may patient waiting for me with a smiling face, and 'without his crotches. I don't think I ever felt so happy in my life. To make a long story short, I attended him closely during the rest of ourvoyag,e—some four days—applying the Oil every night, and guarding him against too much exposure to the fresh and damp spring breezes; and on landing at New York he was able without assistance, to i mount the hotel omnibus and go to the Astor House. I called on him two days later, and found him actually engaged in packing his trunk, preparatory to starting for his home that evening. With a grateful smile he welcomed me, and pointing to a box carefully done up in thick brown paper, he said That is a dozen bottles of, St. Jacobs Oil, which I have just purchased from Hudnut, the chemist across the way, and I am taking them home to show my good mother what has saved her ' son's life and restored him to her in health. If you should ever visit Sedalia, in Missouri, I will show you a bottle of St. Jacobs Oil enshrined in a silver and gold casket, which we shall keep as an ornament, as well as a memento of our meeting on the Cunard steamer.' We parted, after an hour's pleasant chat, with mutual good- will and esteem, and a few weeks afterwards I received a letter from him telling me he was in perfect health, and containing many graceful expressions of his affectionate
regards.

SHIPPING. A Reuter's New York telegram of Tuesday says the storm on the Atlantic seaboard continues with unabated fury, though the weather is warmer. Immense damage has been caused to shipping. The Cunard steamer Etruria had a terribly severe weather experience on her last outward trip, and a sailor named Joseph Wormald was killed by a sea. The Guinn Line steamer Alaska, which arrived at Queenstown on Tuesday night, brings intelligence of the ship Edward, from Havre, to the effect that during a terrible electrical storm eleven of the crew were prostrated on deck by the lightening, and were blind for nearly half a day. The Liverpool ship Duncow, which was abandoned by her crew off Dunkirk under circumstances justifying the , belief that she would become a total wreck, has been taken into Flushing Roads by Belgian fishermen. She had valuable cargo of nitrate from Iquique on board. The abandonment of another Liverpool ship, the Douglas, was also ascertained on Tuesday morning by the arriv,ll at Great Yarmouth of her captain, the pilot, and twenty-three of the crew. The Douglas was abandonad off Heligoland, but at latest accounts she was stil afloat, and tugs had been sent from Hamburg in search. Three of the crew, named D. Jamieson, J. Christianson, and W. Meetens, were drowned. The schooner Dart left Douglas on Tuesday morning in ballast for Liverpool, but two hours later drove ashore at a place called Walberry. The captain and crew saved themselves in their boat. Furious gales are reported from Plymouth, and also from Newcastle. In Liverpool on Tuesday the weather was excessively boisterious. A telegram has been received at Staithes stating that the lifeboat which was supposed to have gone down while succouring the crew of a fishing coble has arrived at Middlesborough with 12 men on board, having been towed thereby a steamer. Only one life has been lost.

LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION IN MANCHESTER. The Marquis of Ripon was present at a Liberal demonstra- tion held on Wednesday night in Chumett-st. Hall, North Manchester. Mr. C. H. Schwann, M.P., presided. Addresses were presented to his lordship on behalf of various political organisations of the district, in reply to which Lord Ripon delivered an address on Irish affairs. Father M`Fadden attended the meeting at a later stage, and spoke in support of a resolution condemning the proposed extension of Lord Ashbourne's Act.

- THE • EXAMINER SATURDAY. DECEMBER 1. 1888.

Mr. L. GORDON RYLANDS, 8.A., son of the late Mr.PErza RYLANDS, M.P., is the author of an ItaPortant work (published by Mr. T. F. lINwIN, London) on "Crime—its Causes and Remedy." he subject is not one which on the face of it Would be likely to attract a comparatively young Writer ; but Mr. RYLANDS comes of a stock that regards difficulties as things to be conquered; 64id he has not hesitated to grapple with a problem Which has been more or less of a puzzle to human- ity since the early days when Cain raised his hand and slew his brother. The work before us is a Painstaking and lucid exposition of views which have been adopted after no• little thought • and research. Those who may not agree with Mr ItYralins' conclusion will be constrained to admit, after reading his book, that he states his case fairly, that lie brings evidence to beer at every Doint that he raises, and that he marshals his facts With conspicuous skill. The inquiry into the causes of crime cannot be said to reveal anything that is really new; but it is pursued with advan- tage in that it strengthens the views of those who 'lave long urged that we must begin with the Young, if we would hope to do anything effectual in the way of thinning the criminal ranks. It 18 common idea that poverty has a great deal to 4.° with crime; but close observation and statis- -4Pal analysis show that this common idea is a

common error. It appears_ from a record of 1,000 criminal cases investigated by the Rev. H. L. ELLIOT, M.A., that 351 first convictiong were traceable to bad company; 205 to drink; 52 to poverty; 77 to opportunity; 67 to want of principle ; 96 to bad temper; 39 to immorality er wantonness; 11 to incapacity and imbecility; and 102 to other causes not specified. It will be seen that bad company is the primary cause of the commencement of a career of crime. It is just possible, however, that further investigation will reduce somewhat the percentage under that head, while increasing the number of those classed under "want of principle." A criminal when cross- questioned will, as a rule, be more likely to Make it out that his "going wrong" was dueto bad com- pany rather than to his own lack of principle. It is a hopeful feature that comparatively few are driven to crime through poverty. It is an indica- tion that the mass of suffering humanity will endure much before resorting to theft to relieve the pangs of hunger. It may be, and doubtless is, the fact that, compared with "the good old times," which were often very boil times, fewer, relatively speaking, of the young feel the pinch of poverty. But there is no denying that the number is still largo ; and it will continue large so long as in our big cities • there are so many with little or no employment, and so many, too, who spend in drink what they ought to devote to feeding, clothing, and educat- ing their children. It is saddening to note that 20 per cent. of first convictions are traceable to drink ; but it is mom than saddening—it is appalling to refielt that—considering offenders as a whole—no less than 75 per cent of the crime of the country is committed under the influence of intoxicating liquor. Mr. RYLANDS does not by any meliffs4ignore the drinlpfactor ; and he quotes statisticsnwhich show that "in abnormally pros- perous Years a great increase of drunkenness is followed by an increase of every kind of offence." He regards drunkenness,when it has become habit- ual, as a disease, and would have it treated as a disease on a scale sufficiently large to warrant the hope that cures could be effected to such an extent as, finally, to reduce the crime of the country. Summing up on the first part of his subject, Mr. RYLAND'S says— The active causes of all crime are these: Defect- ive training or total absence of any; immoral associ- ates and bad example in prison as well as out of it; drink, idleness, and the hereditary transmission of evil tendencies. These causes, however, frequently overlap, and one is often found to be the effect of another. The only perfectly simple and absolutely final division is into two main heads, Heredity and Environment, which comprise all others." Our author next proceeds to deal with the various methods of dealing with crime, and argues—con- clusively as it seems to us—that society has succeeded in reducing the percentage of crime by the reformatory rather than the deterrent system. Since 1845 there hasbeen a steady decline, (not- withstanding the increase in population.) in the number of persons condemned to penal servitude, and Mr. RYLAND'S shows that this decline synchro- nises with the steps that have been taken year by year to educate and reform the class of people from whom hardened criminals are recruited. Reformatory and Industrial Schools have been wonderful agencies for good; and it is therefore proposed to profit by the experience we have obtained, and extend these agencies enormously; Mr. RYLANDS says : . .

_ Now, there is one way, and one way only, by which embryo criminals may be caught and dealt with before inherited tendencies have had time to develop or evil example t.) make itsalf felt, and that is for the State to take under its own abso lute control all children found in the streets without visible means of subsistence, or who seem to be neglected by their parents. This will seem a startling proposition to those who have not given much thought to the subject; but as a matter of fact it is covered by the law— by the Industrial Schools Act—at the present I moment. The weak point is that it is left to I "any person" to enforce the law; Mr. RYLANDS would amend this by making distinct provision for its enforcement. He estimates that there are one million children to whom it would apply, and that the State would need to provide Industrial Schools for this number. The annual cost per head in these schools is 21.5 ; so that we should require £16,000,000 a year to keep them going. This, it must be confessed, is a staggering sum; but it is urged that enforced payments from negli- gent parents, and reduction of expenditure by re- ducing the: criminal and pauper population would soon bring the total down to £8,000,000. The chief question, of course is—Would this annual expenditure of £3,000,0J0 be a good investment? There can be no. doubt that it would, if it were absolutely certain that the scheme would succeed. There is much virtue, to be sure, in the "if," and we fear it will be altogether too much for JOHN Bunn, who cannot as yet be persuaded to spend a million or two more in making education free. But the plan is not one that need be carried out , in its entirety; it can be tried piecemeal as an experiment. Let Government include a specified sum in the estimates for the extension of Industrial Schools; and let the results be care- fully noted. Should it be found that it pays to manufacture good citizens in this particular way, it is a matter of course to say that there will be no difficulty in the long run about providing the requisite millions, Coming to the treatment of adult criminals, Mr. RYLANDS would so classify them as to prevent the very bad making the bad worse. He would reorganize the labour of prisoners, as is done in some places on the contin- ent, with a view to making prison labour pay. But, more than all, he would seek to make prisons rdormatories rather than places of punish- ment. This is not suggested from any sentimen- tal feeling; Mr. RYLANDS shows himself to be a hard matter-of-fact reasoner from beginning to end, and his proposals are well worth considering. We have read his work with great interest; and commend it to all who have at heart the ameliora- tion of the race. It is an important contribution to an important subject ; and it is in every way a credit to Mr. GORDON RYLANDS.

THE Oaths Bill passed through committee -of the House of Lords, on Tuesday, without being altered in .a single clause; and it is pretty safe now to predict that it will, become law. It is not a I particularly good bill; but it is an improvement on the law as it stands, and it is acceptable—just as half a loaf is better than no bread. Mr. BEAD- LAUGH .has been reproached for sticking to his measure after it had been mutilated in the House of Commons, but Mr. BRADLAUGH is above all things a practical politician. He admits that he is not getting all that he ought to have; but he will take what is offered him, and begin again. The object of the bill, as Lord SPENCER described it, is " to -allow certain persons to affirm instead of taking the oath in the cases where oaths are
administered." Unfortunately, before this desir-
able end can be attained, a person who prefers to affirm is practically called upon to declare that he takes this course because he has •no religious belief. This is most offensive; it is a piece of

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA_TURDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1888.

impertinence which will be got rid of when the Oaths Bill comes to be amended, as it will be, when the Liberals return to power. Objectionable as the measure is in this respect, the/LORD CHANCELLOR sought to make it still more objec- tionable by providing that if any juror affirmed under the set 4' it shall be good cause of ehallengo to that juror by the Crown, or by the prisoner in any criminal proceeding, and by any party thereto in any civil cause or matter." From this it will be seen that when the law had, in effect, declared that a juror who affirmed was as good as any other juror, it was intended to leave it to a private individual to challenge him as a person unfit to act as a juror. This speci- men of crass Toryism went to the yobs, but even the House of Lords could not swallow it, the 11 " amendment"—s.we the mark I—being rejectcd by 54 to 14. It was an interesting feature of the gen- eral discussion of the measure to see the. ARCHBISHOP of CANTHRBURY bless the bill in a fatherly sort of way. He admitted that it came to him from many sources that he was expected to ban rather than bless; but it seems that even an Archbishop may come round, after a time, to seo things after the fashion of ordinary common-sense people. He was -not quite consistent with himself, but that was not of much moment; seeing that he didn't go into the wrong lobby. It is apparent, too, that he has been searching the scriptures, and has made the profound discovery that "the Saviour ordered that no oath at all should be taken, and he could not take the ground that it was a.matter of indifference whether an oath more or less was required." We have a dim recollection that a like appeal to the teaching of Christ has been made a hundred times during the past, few years; but it makes all the differ- enee in the world; we suppose, when scripture is quoted by_an Archbishop. Curiously, his grace went on to qualify his itatenieiat by saying "The necessity of the oath was to be deplored." ; But where is the "necessity "—and we put the ques- tion to him as an Archbishop—if "the Saviour ordered that no oath at all should, be taken ?" Does he wisnit to be understood that a necessity may arise for disobeying -a 'specific and, unmistake- able scriptural injunction? Or—to put it in another way—does his grace recognise a higher ' authority than the divine Master he professes to serve? It is this playing fast and loose with the precepts of Christianity which is "to be deplored." It is a bad example when an ignorant Salvationist is .guilty of it; but it is worse still when the offence is committed by ti learned Archbishop. But "something- too much of this." The attempt to serve God and Mammon is no now thing. Let us be thankful for small mercies, for the Arch- bishop of Canterbury can now see his' way to quote scripture, and vote, in favour of the Oaths Bill. Mr. -BRADLAUGH has conquered; he is backed up at lest by the highest dignitary of the English Church.

Mr. G. Shaw-Lefevro has issued a work on the Irish question, with, the title .of ,?• incidents of Coercion." Ho thus sums, up his special experi- ence in Ireland:—"•The Act. of 1887 has been most satisfactory in its operation. so far as it went; it has relegated to the Land &emission future dis- putes as to judical rents, anti aá to leaseholds and town parks, and it has greatly improved the posi- tion of non-judicial tenants. . . There cannot be a doubt that if, it had also dealt with arrears of rent, much of which was due to the delay and neglect of Parliament to legislate in the 1 previous year, all the remaining disputes between landlords and tenants. would have been disposed of, combinations would have ceased, the Plan of Campaign would have disappeared.'

We learn that the .Scretary for the Colonies has received a tele- graphic despatth from the Governor of South Australia, on behalf of the Colonial Ministry, on the subject of the appointment of Colonial Governors. The Ministers state they have no desire to eneroach on the constitutional rights of the Imperial Government; but point out that if the Colonies bad the: power of stating objections to proposed 'appointments, the power would not be,lightly exercised. In other words, they esire to carry out still further the principle of Home Rule. They have no liking, any more than the Irish, of the policy of—" Shut your eyes and open your mouth, and swallow whate'er we send you."

SAD FATALITY AT A FARM AT BOLD.—A farm labourer named Patrick Riley. aged 53 years, employed by Mr. James Houghton, farmer, of Bold, died on Wednesday from injuries, the result of a sad accident the previous day. The farmer and five of his men, deceased being one of them, were I engaged in the shippon putting large flags down I to form partitions. The men were lowering a flag I down, and the deceased was guiding it. Mr. Houghton held the atone in position with a crowbar, and on Riley saying "All right; let go" he drew' the bar out. The stone in falling caught the deceased's head against the wall, fracturing the skull. Dr. Casey, St. Helens, was sent for, but death ensued on Wednesday. COUNTY COUNCIL CANDIDATES.—It will be seen from our advertising columns that more candidates for seats in the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils are in the field for local electoral divisions. Mr. Edward .Greenall, J.P., of Grappenhall Hall, offers his services to the electors of the Dares- bury _ division. lie points out that he has , acted as a magistrate for nearly 23 years, having served on the County Police and Licensing Committees for some years, and also that he has been chairman of the Daresbury Highway Board for 20 years. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., of The Highlands, Runcorn, comes forward for the division of Runcorn south, in response to a request signed by a numerous and influential body of electors: I.le refers to his life-long connection and residence in Runcorn, and to his services a; a magistrate on the County Committee. For the suffrages of the Frodsham division Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., of Netherton, is a candidate. In his address he alludes to his former experiences as a tenant' farmer and tanner, and t his twelve years services as a magistrate, as some guarantee of his fitness Jot the position he seeks to fill.

MR. E. R. RUSSELL AT WIDNES. On Thursday night, to inaugurate the opening of the ne,w Lecture Hall of the, Widnes Liberal Club, and also a series of lectures, Mr. E. R. Russell, of Liverpool, delivered an address on "The present aspect of the Irish Question" to a large and appre- ciative audience at the Widnes Liberal Club. Mr. Eustace Carey occupied the chair, and supporting him, in addition to Mr. Russell, were Mr. J. Morrison (the president of the club), Drs. 0 Keeffe and Hutchinson, Messrs. H. B. Shores (Liberal agent for the district), J. Ileyes, C. Finn, T. Hartland, J. Beach, J. roole, J. Marsh, F. Cave (lion. sec.), &c. Mr. J. Morrison, at the outset of the proceedings, briefly explained the objects of the club and its financial position. The total cost of furnishing the club amounted to £2OO, and he was pleased to say that the leading Liberals of the town and the rank and file of the party had supported them in a most generous manner. (Applause.) The Chairman congratulated them heartily upon the success of the club up to the present. This success, he felt sure, was greatly due to the exertions of the president and secretary. The subject on which they were to be addressed was one lyinz near to their hearts, and he the chairman) was perfectly satisfied, as a politician, to let everything rest until the great question of Ireland was settled. He was quite willing to allow any question to stand aside until the Irish difficulty was settled, and on those persons who postponed the settle- ment of that question, by their wretched policy in Ireland. rested, he thought, the whole responsibility of postponing a number of measures which were wanted very much in England and the colonies. There were other measures requiring to be j;iassed which were getting over ripe. The question as to the Government of India was ripening very fast, but they could net touch it until they had concluded the task of ameliorat- ing the condition of the people of Ireland. (Applause.) Mr. E. R. Russell was then introduced to the meeting, and was greeted with loud applause, . which was fre- quently renewed during the delivery of his address. Ile congritulated the members of the IVidnes Liberal Club on the desire which thee evinced in the selection of the subject to be well posts in the Irish question to the very date at which they met. There were, he said, many things in the past to encourage them thus to settle for themselves the rights and wrongs of matters at particu- lar points in the progress of this great question. Liberals were frequently told that all their past exertions for Ireland had bees useless. • But if they had carefully watched Irish affairs for years past, they would be ' ready to reply that all their exertions had been hampered ' by defects and compromises to which they objected when they were adopted, and which they prophesied would be fatal to anything like complete success. It would be time enough to despair when they had passed any really great measure for Ireland without conces- sions to Ireland's enemies both here and in her own country. The mischief was that England would scarcely ever do the right thing at the right time for Ireland, and the reason was the worst possible—namely, that the interests or prejudices of certain classes in this country stood in the way. The latest aspeet of the land question in Ireland was the renewal of the Ashbourne Act, with a new £5,000,000 grant. The Conservatives would take credit for this as if it were a splendid effort on behalf of the Irish tenants. But how came it that the Irish Landlords were so eager for this measure to pass? Perhaps this might be explained by a bill which had been circulated during the Holborh election, and which stated that from the ex tention of the Ashbourne Act sums of £400,000, £267,000, £260,000, £170,000, and £400,000 were to be apportioned among the London City Companies, the Duke of Aber- corn, the Duke of Leinster, the Marquis of Bath, Lord Lurgan and Lord Londonderry. In as many as 1,200 cases, however, the Land Commissioners

had refused to ratify Asihourne Act contract; beernse they were on wrongprinciples ; and it has been alleged in the House of Commons that £240,000 had been paid for lands which the Land Commissioners considered gave security only for £180,006: There was only one argument for the new Ashbourne Bill, which was Lord Randolph Churchill's—that it was a Tittle one. What was very puzzling was thatphilosepliical politicians should be led by fear of Home Rule to tolerate measures so utterly unfir.--for the circumstances, co insular and Philistine. A pressing and immediate • matter was what might be called the foreign and colonial aspect of the Irish difficulty. Our Irish relations were now poisoning our diplomacy and our colonial governznent. We had this year. suffered two humiliations entirely arising out eighe Irish question. One was the dismissal of our ambassador from America. It was no use our saying we liked this, because we di sl not like it. We liked it all the less because we had practically brought it on ourselves. It had been btrosight upon us mainly by the,• selection of Mr. Chamberlain as the envoy •of this country when any diplomatist knowing his business would have said that he was a very bad ' helection. However, it might be thought that we Could afford to quarrel with the United States. What we could not afferdi to, do, and what it was evident the Government %knew we could not afford to do, was to quarrel with our colonies. Sir Henry Blake having been nominated as-Governor of Queensland had had to be withdrawn. LorePSalisbury's Ministry had to climb down. (Hear, hear) What was the moral of all this ? That all neglect of duty such as we had been guilty of in Ireland broadened out be even innocent consequenees and without ill-meaning over a great area of affairs. It might saturate our whole system with world wide difficulties. We had already seen the moral sense of the Irish peopleeendangered by our toleration of a condition of things in. that country which allowed and almost necessitated the growth of secret societies and the abominable outrages by which they maintained their power; and now weewerelikely to see bitterness arising. all over the world wherever any colonial population was considerably permeated by Irish feeling. (Hear, hear. and applause.) Mr. J. Morrison afterwards moved, and Mr. F. Heyes seconded, a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Russell for his acdress. The motinn having been unanimously carried and briefly acknowledged by Mr. Russell, the meeting closed with a similar compliment to the chairman, on the motion of T. O'Keetle, seconded by Mr. F. Cave.

DEATH OF MR. R. B. TOFT, OF RUNCORN. The death, oE Mr. Richard Bent Toft, at hes resi- dence, Laur.e• Bank, Garston, is announce 4. Mr. Toft, who had attained the age of 63 years, had been concocted with Runcorn from his early man- hood, and was weil known and highly respected by an extensive _circle of the inhabitants. He was a ship owner on a large scale, and carried on the business of a ship broker, besides being con- nected with several public undertaking:. He was a member of the Board of Directors at the Gas Works, and up to ak few months ago was auditor to the Waterworks Company. At one time he took a 'great interest in the local government of the town, but of late years he had taken no part in these affairs. He had been in fitts health for a considerable period, and had been co tabis residence since May last, his death taking place on Tuesday. His remains were interred at Garston Church Yesterday, when a large number of friends and relatives paid their last respects at the grave side.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TurADAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. ; LIVING ix SrYl3l.—Mr. Arthur Linaker. solicitor, appeared in support of a judgment summons issued by Messrs. Alexander and Shepherd, against William Garner, of Halton.—John Frodsham, called, said he knew Garner was a commission agent and lived in a large house at Halton, having two acres of land attached. He drove about Runcorn in a phaeton drawn by a pony.—The Judge: He may be over head and ears in debt and still live in that style.—Mr. Linaker He must keep the pony and trap out of something.—The Judge: He may not ; that is the very thing. The Judge remarked fthat Garner was up hat court day and he did not seem to have any means. He declined to make an order upon the defendant, who did not appear. Hann cm THE PAWNBROXER.—WiIIiam Leach, quarry manager, Albert-street, Runcorn, sued Arthur Davies, pawnbroker, tligh-stroet, for £2, value of a silver watch and chain pawned with the defendant and belonging to the plaintiff.—Mr. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the defendant.—Froni the statement of the plaintiff, it appeared that he had a license to deal in watches and jewellery and he entrusted a man, whose name did not transpire, with a number of watches and chains to sell for him. The man betrayed the confidence reposed in him by pawning the whole of the articles, and then absconding, but he was afterwards apprehended and Was sentenced to 9 months hard labour at the Quarter Sessions. The plaintiff ascertained that four pawn- brokers in Runcorn had received his articles in pledge and he offered to redeem them by paying one half. Three of the pawnbrokers accepted this offer, but the defend- ant refused to give -up the watch and chain in his possession unless he were paid the whole amount for which the articles were pledged.—Mr. Humphreys argued that if the plaintiff was entitled to the goods it was clearly subject to the amount which had been advanced upon them by the pawnbroker. He said there were' many decisious in county courts which upheld his Contention. After an argument between the advocate and judge, the latter said the plaintiff's agent was only empowered to sell, he had no power to pawn; and the pawnbroker took the articles with the title the man had to give. If the pawnbreker was deceived the loss fell upon him.—The defendant was ordered to return the watch and chain in a week,or pay £2 damages and costs. • _

A BORROWING Taawsacrron.—John Blundell, publican, Runcorn, sued Henry Williams, master mariner, King- st., for the sum of £4 2s. 3d. alleged to have been paid on defendant's behalf on a promissory note.—Mr. Wynne Humphreys was for the plaintiff and Mr. J. Burton for the defendant.--Mr. Humphreys stated that a man named Thomas Smith borrowed £lO from John Henry Harrison, and he signed a promissory note for the amount. The plaintiff and defendant signed the note as sureties. Smith repaid a certain amount on account, and an action was brought against Blundell to recover the remainder with the result that he had paid £8 4s. 6d. into court. Blundell now claimed that Captain Williams should pay his share.—Mr. Burton said Smith was a stranger to Williams, who only signed the note at the request of Blundell, who said Smith could not get the money until he had two sureties. He quoted a CAN: to prove that a person who became a surety at the request of another surety was not liable.— After hearing the evidence, his Honour said it was clear that Williams became surety as an accommodation for Blundell, and he must give judgment for the defendant. A CLAIM By BaswEns.—Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., brewers, Wilderspool, sued Edward Hill, insurance agent, Ditton, for £24 175., for beer supplied whilst the defendant was tenant of the Friendship Tavern, Fryer- St., and also for rent due.—Mr. ArthurLinaker appeared for the plaintiffs.—Owing to the absence of a witness the claim for rent was withdrawn.—Two carters proved the delivery of the beer, and the defendant stated that when he left the house in July, 1887, he paid Mr. Laith- waite, the plaintiffs' agent, £l7 in settlement of all claims, and he produced two receipts in support of the statement.—Mr. J. H. Clarke, the cashier, said these receipts were fer rent. He asked why Mr. Laithwaite was not brought forward as a witness ?—Mr. Linaker said Mr. Laithwaite had lost his memory and was not fit to appear in Court.—His Honbur said evidence was con- clusive that the defendant owed for the beer, and gave judgment for £2l us.
WOUNDING A WIFE AT WIDNES.
EXTRAORDINARY DOMESTIC RELATIONS.

At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, William Sant, labourer, of 44 Victoria-street, was charged with wounding his wife, Sarah Ann, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm.—Mary McLean, wife of George McLean. who occupies the parlour in prisoner's house, deposed that on the afternoon of the 20th November Mrs. Sant was 4 drunk, and fell asleep on the . floor. When the prisoner arrived home she heard him breaking the furniture, and afterwards saw Mrs. Sant strike him and run away into the lobby. Mrs. Sant cried out "0, Mary, he has killed me." She found Mrs. Sant bleeding from the head.—The prosecutrix said on the day in question her husband forced is. 6d. from her. He then went out and did not return until evening. In the meantime witness got drunk, and as she had not the tea ready, her husband began to break the furniture. She then struck him on the head with the poker or a table leg. Seeing she had caused her husband's head to bleed, she ran away, but tripped and fell in the lobby. While she lay there her husband kicked her on the side and she became unconscious. She had since suffered great pain. She had provoked her husband by getting drunk and refused to get hie tea. She had frequently been abused by her husband.—Dr. O'Keeffe described the wound on the woman's head, which must have required great 'violence. She was bruised on the body, and had internal pain. She was not yet out of danger.—r.c.McGinis said he went to the prisoner's house and asked the woman how her head was wounded. Shereplied that her husband had kicked her. Prisoner said he would not go to the Police Station without a warrant, and if the constable attemp ed to take him " he would put his clogs as deep into him." He went quictly.—The prisoner was com- mitted to the Assizes fortrial.

The "World" says :—" Mach anxiety is felt about the health of the Czarina. Although the real state of affairs is concealed is much as pos- sible, it is now an open secret that she has never recovered the terrible shock to her nerves caused by the recent railway accident."

Is there or is there not a nuisance caused by the 'Warrington Intercepting Depots?- It is about time this question was settled in a definite man- ner. It is suggestive that those who live (or shall we say, survive) near them say they are a nuisance. But there is to be an official inquiry, is there not? The public have had the promise; they are waiting now for the performance.

It is a matter of course for 'sundry Irish mem- bers to be imprisoned, but the monotony of the proceeding has been varied by putting an English M.P. in "the stone jug." This is Mr. Gent- Davis, who is a hard up and defaulting trustee. He is the Tory representative of Kennington Division, London. Couldn't the electors find a better man? They may have the opportunity of trying before very long.

The " progressives " in matters educational have gained in the London School Board elec- tions, though not sufficiently to set aside the old policy. Mr. Diggle, late chairman of the Board, is returned, but it is a warning to him that he stands fourth on the list for Marylebono. Mr. Conybeare, M.P., is returned for Finsbury, and Mrs. Annie Besant is first on the poll for Tower Hamlets. The Liberals have shown themselves alive, and have polled well. London is looking up.

It looks as if there were going to be a struggle for the honour of representing the various divisions in the new County Councils. And there might be a worse -thing for the ratepayers than that. It will ensure them getting to know some- thing about the new Act, and something, too, about the views of the candidates. In any case, arrangement or no arrangement, candidates would cicii,o come before the public, and show, if they can, that they are made of "sterling stuff."

Life is not "all beer and skittles" with the Dissentient Liberals. According to the "Daily News" the pressure for pairs among them is increasing. They cannot, of course pair with Conservatives, and the general feeling on the Liberal benches is against pairing with gentlemen who sit on the Liberal side and habitually vote with the Government. The consequence is that Dissentient Liberals are obliged either to remain in attendance throughout the night,or to reduce the Ministerial majority by abstention from divisions.

The Van and Wheel tax has been too much for the Chahcellor of the Exchequer. Mr. Smith announced, on Wednesday, that the. Government did not intend to proceed any further with the bill. Mr. Goschen has always talked as if nothing would cause him to abandon his bantling; but what does that amount to? Is he not himself an abandoned politican ? Mr. Conybeare suggested that he should resign; but the Chancellor of the Exchequer has swallowed bigger things than this wheel tax in order to keep in office. He will not resign.

Church schools are beginning to compete with theatres. It is not long since a dramatic license was applied for on behalf of St. James's, Warring- ton, and now a similar license has been obtained for Christ Church schools. im It will see to some i like a new departure ; but t s really a revival. In the olden time plays under the sanction and direction of the Church were the order of the day. We do not know that it can be said that plays are to be produced at the Latchford schools; but "something of the kind" is to be pre- sented. And a good thing, too, if the entertain- ment be really good.

• There are plenty of nuts for the Fair Traders to crack. The other week it was stated in the French Chamber that as a result of "Protection," French bakers had gone over the border into Belgium. They found they could send cheap breed into France, but not cheap four. Still the bread must be dearer than it ought to be. And noto we hear of a Yankee Screw Company removing to M Canada to avoid excessive import duties. r. Henry George thinks the Americans are learning on the Free Trade Question, but the 7 are learning slowly. The weakness of Protection is that— speaking of a country as a whole—it does not protect. •

Mort Liddell and Co., when he slipped from a plank into a vat of hot liquor. His legs and feet were badly scalded,and he was at once conveyed to the Accident Hospital in a cab. "AN brrsavisw wmt A SCEPTIC.' —The Rev. R. G. Hughes, paster of the Milton Congregational Church, Widnes, preached the third of a series of special sermons OR Sunday evening. The above was he title of his dis- course, which was based upon Hebrews xi: ; and Mr. Hughes dealt with the fundamental principles of the Christian religion. GOSPEL UNION HALL, WIDNES.—Miss Perry and Miss York, the eszangelists recently appointed to take charge of the Widnes Gospel Mission, conducted special services in this building on Monday. In the evening a ' service of song entitled "The Torn Bible" was rendered by an efficient choir and band, under the leadership of Mr. George Bullivant. Mrs. Robinson, of Hope House, , Farnworth' read the narrative. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Clank, of Hough Green. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPEItANCE SOCIETY, WIDNES. 1 —An instructive and interesting lectnre in connection with the above society was delivered in the Waterloo- road Schools, on Thursday evening, by the Rev. George Henry St. Patrick Garrett, B.D. the subject of his dis- course being" A Tour in Norway." The lecture was illustrated by beautiful limelight views by Mr. J. B. Imison. Mr. Garrett's knowledge of• Norway gathered from his visits, and the graphic accounts Ve gave of them, kept the audience highly interested for nearly two hours. LACEY-ST. BAND OF HOPE. WIDNES.—The usual weekly meeting of the members of this society, was held on Monday evening. The Rev. T. Law presided, and there was a capital audience of young people. An interesting programme was gone through, and was much enjoyed. Recitations were given by Sarah J. Hartland, Sarah Ann Forster, Kato Robinson. Annie Knight, Alfred Hackney and George F. Hartland, whilst solos were rendered by Miss Poulson and Mr. Dodd, A party of Baptist friends also contributed several musical items. A collection was made at the conclusion of the entertainment. A YOUNG THIEF AT RUNCORN.—Joseph Nicholls' ages! 12;years, whose home is in Parker-st.,was brought before the Runcorn magistrate on Monday, charged with stealing a watch worth £l, belonging to Harry Crow' watchmaker, Ashridge-st., Duke's Field. ft appeared that the boy was employed as errand boy by Mr. Vaug- han. watchmaker, Vicar-st., and on the 20th ult, he was sent to the prosecutor's shop. Afterwards, a boy who said he was sent by his father, offeied a watch in pledge to Mr. Davies, who told the boy to fetch his father. The boy did not return and it was discovered that the prisoner had stolen the watch from the prosecutor's shop.—The prisoner was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod. SAVAGE ATTACK ON A GIRL AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, a married woman named Dowse, of 1, Nelson-st., was charged with having unlaWfnlly wounded a girl, ten years of age, named Julia McKay. It appeared that the family of McKay have lodged at the prisoner's for Some time; and on Monday a dispute arose between the prisoner and the girl. During the contention Mrs. Dowse took up an empty meat can, and with this struck the girl several blows pn the top and side of the head. The edges of the tin were very sharp, and severe scalp wounds were inflicted on the head, while the ehoeks were bruised. Dr. Hutchinson was sent for, and on the arrival of that gentleman the girl presented a fearful spectacle, blood having issf4B from the wound in streams. He stitched and dressed the wounds, and ordered her removal to bed. As the unfortunate girl 'was unable to appear, the magistrates remanded the prisoner for a week. FELONIES AT WIDNES.—A labourer named John Crozier was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday charged with stealing a cap worth 6d., the property of Peter McKinley, smallware dealer, St. Helens.—Mr. McKinley occupies a stall in Widnes market, and on Saturday evening, John Hoole, his assistant, saw the prisoner take the cap and place it on his head, under his hat. The prisoner was followed and given into the custody of P.C. Massey. He pleaded guilty and asked the magistrates to take into consideration the fact that he was drunk at the time A fine of 20s. was imposed; or in default 14 days' imprisonment.—Annie Jones, who said she came from Walsall, Staffordshire, was charged with having stolea three neckerchiefs, worth Is. 74d., the property of F. Tebbutt, draper, 53 Ann-st. West. The prisoner was seen by a girl named Catherine Riley to snatch the articles from the shop door and run away. She was afterwards apprehended by P.C. MeGinis and said "I did not Steal them; I found them in the street." The woman now informed the Bench that she was drunk at the time, and she was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

POACHINdar Oft sPeßniar..l..—Joseph Leigh,labourer,Apule- ton,was charged with having had inhis possession one hare and eleven rabbits which had been unlawfully obtained on the 9th November.—P.C. Millington said that about twenty minutes pasi six on Friday morning, the 9th November, he was pro- ceedingalong Knutsford-road at Grappenball when he met defendant and another man walking in the direction of War- rington. Defendant was carrying a bag, and the other man appeared to have somethifig bulky in his pockets. As soon as witness came in sight the second man ran off. Witness asked defendant what he had in his bag, The reply was "Nothing." but on searching the bag the officer found in it one hare and eleven rabbits. Defendant said he got them from his own land at Appleton. He afterwards said , " Twill tell the truth. This is the first time I have been caught. I have been and fetched the rabbits this morning, and Mr. Barber gave me the hare." The rabbits and the hare were quite warm. Cross-examined Witness afterwards saw Mr. Barber, who said he had given the hare to the defendant two days before,—For the defence, Mr. Arthur Browne sub- mitted that there was no case against against his client, bias- much as the summons was bad.—The objections were over- ruled by the Bench, and Mr. Browne then called William Barber, of Appleton, who said that on the 7th November he met the defendant and gave him a hare which he had found that morning on the moss. Mr. Middleton had given defend- ant permission to shoot rabbits on his land.—The Bench con- sidered the case proved, and inflicted a fine of 40s. and costs, or, in default, one month's imprisonment with hard labour.— Mr. Browne gave notice of appeal. Subeequently Howard scored after a good run, and from this point of the game until the call of time play was constantly in the Birch quarters, and tries were obtained by Howard, Hardman and Gandy. Plimpton, and i".• Hewitt secured trieS, while Plurrapton (2) and Farrell placed goals The final sesta stood :—WistasS. 5 goals, 7 tries, and 8 minors, to nothing Sr. Flimess "A" V. FIIODEINAIL—The return match between these clubs was played at Frodsham before 500 spectators. Frodsham brass band played selections of music during the game. The home team having wen the toss decided to play down hill. Brownbill kicked off. (with the vrind) for the risitors, When the whistle sounded for half time. Frodsham was leading by one minor to the Saints nil. Tudor restarted for the home team, arid some tall kicking was exchanged between the opposing backs. From a bit of loose play the home team registered another minor. After which Edwards passed to McNally, who ran from behind his own twenty- five right down the touch line, and gained a magnificent try, for which he was loudly applauded. Brownbill took the place, and made a grand attemp the ball strik- ing the posts. Directly afterwards time was called, the game ending in a win for St. Helens after a hard fought game by one try and one minor, to Frodsham two minors.

HuNcons v. ROCHDALE HORNETS (.4 A" TnAms.)—The Runcorn second team paid a visit to Rochdale on Satur- day. Starting from Runcorn at 12 o'clock, they arrived in Rochdale in goad time. The ground was in a very sloppy state, and almost unfit to play upon. Under the circumstances, however, some very good play was shown, and an interesting, though unsatisfactory, game was witnessed by a goodly number of spectators. As to the respective merits of the teams, the Runcorn backs were far superin to those of the home team, and the forwards could not only hold their ovra in the scrimmage, but were faster on the loose. The score does not indicate the real nature of the game, as Runcorn earned two tries which were disallowed, besides not being allowed to kick for goal after another try. Crompton. Davies, and Cawley, scored the tries for Runcorn. Mr Crosby,of Manchester, was the referee and the game ended, Rochdale Hornets, one goal, 1 try, and 2 minors; to Runcorn, 3 tries, and 3 minors.

WARR/NOTON "A" TRAMv MANCESSTHR ATHLTMO. The above clubs met en the Warrington ground, which at one part was in a very wet condition, on Saturday. Two thirties being agreed upon, Appleton (captain of the home team) won the toss and elected to play with the wind in his favour. Fox kicked off for the visitors. Boardman was tackled before he could return, and passed to Lawless, who kicked to the visitors' 25. From a scrimmage the Athletic took tho ball to Warrington quarters, Boardman and Speakman relieved the pres- sure. From a scrimmage Mather passed to Speakman. who got away, but lost possession of the ball, and Appleton picking up, ran round his opponents, but owing to the slippery state of the ground could not keep his footing. Stretton put in a good kick to BOSCOW, who returned to touch. From the line out the home forwards broke away, and Rigby kicked to Boscow, who returned well to centre. Play raged in neutral territory for some time, several scrimmages taking place, from one of which Russell and Gregory broke away and carried play to the Warringtou line, Boscow averting danger by a good kick to centre. Appleton made a short kick and followed up, but was collared by Cope. Donoghue, Molyneaux, and Isherwood dribbled up the field from a line-out, but Okell relieved by a good kick to Boscow, who returned well to tench. Several line-outs took place in succession, from one of which the Athletic forwards broke away and dribbled nicely to centre, where play rested for some time. Isherwood, Warburton, and Holmes headed a grand dribble up the field, Harper saving. After give and take play Rigby checked a dangerous rush near the visitors' 25, and relieved by a good kick. McGowan soon afterwards got the ball away with a nice run, but was tackled by Boardman. The Warrington forwards broke away, and carried play to the visitors' goal line, enabling Lawless ' to get over, but he was tackled by Rigby and a maul ensued, from which Lawless came off victorious. Isher- wood made a good attempt for goal, the ball just falling short. Fox dropped out, the ball going in touch. From the line-out Isherwoed was collared, and a scrimmage formed, from which Russell,Cope, and Gregory dribbled to Warrington 25, forcing Warrington to kick dead. Appleton dropped out, and the forwards following up well caused play to rest in the centre. Good passing was now indulged in by the Warrington backs, Apple- ton putting in a kick and, followiag up, tackled his man before he could part with the oval. Speakman soon afterwards took at drop a goal, the ball just going under- neath the bar, and Rigby replied by a kick into touch. From the lino-out Russell got away, Speakman saving. The whistle blew for half time, the score stand- ing Warrington one try, Athletic one minor. In the opening of the second half the Athletic, having the wind in their favour, played up and from a scrimmage Wil- liams got over for the Athletic. Fox made a good attempt at goal. After this, however, Vtarrington began to press, and from a scrimmage Mather passed to Apple- ton, who rounded his opponents and placed the ball between the posts. Warburton took the place kick, and landed a goal. Speakman soon after forced a minor. The visitors carried play to the Warrington 25, and Boscow relieved to centre. From the line-out the visitors' forwards dribbled up the field, Boscow secur- ing. Play was carried to the home line, and a scrim- mage formed under the posts. The Warrington for- wards relieved. From a scrimmage in the visitors' 25, Mather secured and dashed over the line, Warburton again doing the needful. The whistle now blew for "No side,' the score being• as follows :—Warrington, 2-1-1 ; Manchester Athletic, 0-1-1. Teams :—War- rington: Full back, Boscow; three-quarter backs, Aupleton (captain), Speakznan, and Boardman; half backs. Lawless and • Mather; forwards, Isherwood, Donoghue, Molyneaux, Bate, Warburton, Holmes, Beard, Acton, and Rowe. Manchester Athletic: Full back, Rigby; three-quarter-backs, Skelton, Okell, and McGowan; half backs, Harper (captain), and Fox ; forwards, Watkinson, Williams, Neary, Gregory, Cope, Fawcett, Cowsill, Burke, and Russell. The Maoris beat Liverpool and District in a football match at Fairfield. on Wednesday, by a goal, six tries, and three minors to nothing. The match between Lancashire and Yorkshire, whick took place on Saturday at Whalley Range, was looked forward to with unusual interest, and it is estimated that 10,000 spectators witnessed the game. The interest was largely due to the prevalence of an opinion that ia merits the teams were pretty evenly balanced, and that, therefore, a tight contest would be the result of the meet- ing. In this, however, the supporters of the Lancashire teem were sadly out of it, for rarely kas a county game been more ono-sided. The Yorkshiremaa in some respeets seers I. have done pretty much as they liked, and by the end of thi game piled up the rattling score of four goals, errs tries and 15 minors to three isinore.

There SOCTI3 little doubt that after a defeat of this sort, there will have to be some re-organization in the Lancashire team, and especially in the back departraent. Complaint has more than once been made that the County Committee stick parsistently te old players wise have dens good work in their day but are aot now at their beat and, it is a common imprestioa that a larger Infusion of new blood would be a great advantage. It may be expected that opinions of this sorb will find a pretty loud expression after the display of Saturday last.

We notice that W. Dillon, the Warrington captain, who was one of the Lancashire forwards, is very favourably spokes of in some influential quarters as ono of tite Nest representatives of the home county. Dillon's merits as a player of the first rank are well-known in Warrington, and it is satisfactory to find that they are also receiving full recognition at the hands of his county. The match of to-day is one ef the great events on the Warrington Club's programme, al they are to join issue with the famous Wakefield Trinity on their own ground. The excellent form of the local players is shown by the fact that they have only been once beaten this season, the single defeat being largely attributed to a temporary weaknesa of the team. The game of this afternoon against the great Torkshire combination should be full of exciting Incident.

div.head: BOY CHARGED WITII MURDER IN
div.p: A BOY CHARGED WITII MURDER IN
HAMPSHIRE.

An indescribable sensation has been caused in the Emsworth district by the diseovery of an atrocious murder committed on Monday evening, in the Fairfield, Havant. The victim, a lad named Set-le, aged 13 years, was playing in the Fairfield, when he was suddenly attacked by someone, who seized him and cut his throat from ear to ear, leaving the dead body on the spot where it fell. I lad named Husband gave the alarm. The police and people turned out in large numbers, and the neig,kbourhood was scoured in the hope of finding the murderer. Shortly after seven o'clock a man was arrested by Sergeant Knapton at the railway gatee, Emsworth, on suspicion of being concerned in the murder. He was respectably dressed, wore a sealskin cap, and a long coat. He had dark wkiskers and a small mous- tache, and was carrying a small bundle. He showed great nervous excitement when arrested, and declined to answer the questions put to him. The boy Husband asserted that he saw the prisoner near the scene of the murder.
Thomas Clark, an engine titter, the man arrested on fiu6picion, W 94 brought up before the magistrate on Tuesday, wad diccharged, there being no evidence against him.

The inquest on the boy Searle was opened on Wednes- day aiad adjourned. The boy Husband, who first gave information of the tragedy, was arrested in suspic- ion. It is stated that the bloodstained bide which was found near the scene of the II unitr has been identified as belonging be Husband's brother. Robert Husband, aged 11, was charged at Havant on Thursday with the murder ef Percy Knight Searle, on Monday evening.—Sergeant Knipton deposed to finding the body and,the knife. llrisland told him he sew a ctsange man beatiug the deceased. On Wednesday witness visited Husband for the second time, and found islosid stains on his scarf aud shirt, and arrested him. Evidence of the knife having been in the aocused's possessios having been given, the case was adjourned.

div.head: A. BOY DROWNED AT DOBBY'S LOCKS.
div.p: A. BOY DROWNED AT DOBBY'S LOCKS.

On Saturday morning a boy named James Lawlor six years of age, the son of Michael Lawlor, a labourer, who lives at 84, Orford-lane, was drowned in the Bridgewater Canal, near Bobby's locks, on the township of Poulton. The circumstances if, his death were inquired into by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-west Lancashire, and a jury, at the Marquis of Granby Inn, Church-st., Warrington, on Monday evening.—The father of the deceased said that he last saw him alive on Saturday morn- ing.—Mary Lawlor, the mother, said that about ten o'clock on Saturday morning she saw the deceased playing near the house with some other children of an age similar to his own. Soon after noon she heard that he had been drowned in the canal, and his dead body was brought home at about two o'clock in the afternoon. She had never known him to go so far away from home before.— William Henry Heald tl2), son of William Heald, bricksetter, 48, 11e.rdy-street, said that on Satur- day morning deceased, himself, and two other lads, followed a drove of cattle as far as Manchester- . road. They then went to the turnbridge near to Dobson's locks. Three boys were on the opposite side of the canal, and they were moving the , bridge. When it was opened for about two feet, the deceased jumped on, and then jumped back again, lie made a run preparatory to jumping on the bridge a second time, but the lads on the other side opened it wider, and he alighted in the water. Edgar Taylor, one of the boys with witness, held a stick out to deceased, who grasped it. He, however, let go his hold, sank, and was drowned. Witness then informed the lock-keeper of what had occurred. Witness did not know who the boys were who opened the bridge. The lock-: keeper had told them to go away.—William Edgar Taylor, (10) son of William Taylor, Bfl Orford-lane, ; gave corroborative .evidence. He said in answer to ; ' questions, that the boys who opened the bridge ran away when deceased fell into the water and did not assist to get him out. Witness did not know the I boys—John Rath bone, the lock-keeper, deposed to finding the body of the deceased, and said that he had previously ordered a number of children away I from the vicinity of the canal.—The jury returned I a verdict to the effect that the deceased waa acci- dently drowned.

SOCIAL GATHERING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

On Saturday evening, at the invitation of Councillor J. H. Fleming, a number of the members of the IVarrington Liberal Club sat down in the meeting-room to an excellent tea. Mr. Mitchell, the manager of the club, had done the catering, which was in every way satisfactory, and it may be added that the tables were neatly decorated. Following upon tea, a number of toasts were proposed and I responded to, that of "The Queen and Royal Family" being given by Mr. :Fleming, who, as host, occupied the chair, the vice-chair being occupied by Councillor F. A. Roberts. The toast of "The Liberal Club" was proposed by Mr. W. Long, J.P., who remarked that, although at the present moment he was not quite in agreement with the bulk of the Liberal party as to its Irish policy, yet he felt that they could all come together with the best of feeling at a social gathering of that kind. He was persuaded that clubs of that character were calculated, when properly conducted, to be a source of strength to the party, and he had every wish for the success of the Warrington Liberal' Club. Mr. ; Fleming responded, saying that so long as he held , office as president he should do all that lay in his power to serve the club, and he trusted that his efforts would be seconded by the members. He I urged that an effort should be made to increase the membership, as a large number of Liberals in the town would doubtless identify themselves with the , club if they were asked to become members. Mr. John Walker then proposed the health of "The President of the Liberal Association," remarking upon the great indebtedness of the Liberal party to the long and eminent services of their esteemed president, Mr. J. G. McMinnies. The toast was received with musical honours,and Mr. Whinnies, in responding, expressed the hope that there would be an end before long to the division in the Liberal party, and tnen they could go forward unitedly to the great work in the way of reform which still lay before them. Ile believed that they had every reason to take courage with regard to their position in Warrington. The register was well looked after, and they would bo able to give a good account of themselves whenever they were called upon to take part in a general election. "Success to ihe Liberal party" was proposed by Mr. Thomas Birchall. who said that Liberalism was identified with everything that was for the pro- gress and the benefit of humanity. Councillor. F. A. Roberts responded, and dwelt upon the position and prospects of tho party in the borough, express- ing his willingness at all times, as Chairman of the Executive, to assist the party in every pos- sible way. The toast of "Our Host," the Chair- man, was proposed by Councillor W. Pierpoint, who commented upon the good qualities of Mr. Fleming, and said that he was quite convinced, when he himself resigned office as president of the club, that they would find that his successor would be theright man in the right place. Musical honours having been awarded to the toast, Mr. Fleming briefly responded, remarking that he wished to say nothing about himself beyond that he trusted that it would be found when he retired from office that he had done the best that he could for the club. The toast of the "Vice-presidents" was proposed by Mr. David Tinnion, and responded to by Dr. Gornall, J.P., and Mr. A. Browne, who con- cluded by proposing a vote of thanks to the manager, Mr. Mitchell, for the satisfactory way in which he had provided and served tea. The proceedings con- cluded with the passing of a,vote of thanks to Mr. Fleming for his hospitality, on the proposition of Mr. Walker, seconded by Mr. C, J. Holmes. During the evening, songs were:given by Messrs. T. Birchall, James Locker, Thomas Cooper, J. E. Warren, D. Tinnion, and J. Clayton, and recitations were given by Messrs. S. Kenyon and T. Cooper.

CARDINAL NEWMAN AND Mn. GLADSTONE.— The "Dublin Evening Mail's "London correspondent says Mr. Gladstone was specially pleased at Birmingham by the following incident, hitherto unreported :—" A note, written in a feeble scrawl, was brought to him from Cardinal Newman, who wrote that he was very ill, but he sent Mr. Glad- stone his blessing." These simple words produced a profound impression on Mr. Gladstone, who insisted on delivering his reply with his own hand. has. S. A.
