CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &C. "Commodore Junk " is the title of a new story by Mr. G. Manville Fenn, which is published by Messrs. Cassell and Co. Like most of this versatile author's works, it is a stirring tale of adventure, the scene being laid, in the first place, on the Devonshire coast, but afterwards transferred to the West Indiei, where the principal characters have an exciting time of it. As" Commodore Junk" is a pirate, it will be understood that there is a good deal of fighting; but the story is also a story of love, of the constant and heroic kind. The characters are not numerous, but they are finely drawn, and present themselves to the reader as creatures of flesh and blood, in whose fortunes he cannot but take deep interest. The volume is well printed and handsomely bound ; it is published at 55., and makes a gift book which is sure to prove acceptable.

" the Wonders of Animal Instinct," from Cassell's Library of Wonders, is a book which young or old may read with pleasure awl profit. It is from the French of Ernest Menault • it abounds with anecdotes, and is amply illustrated. Its popularity and value as a shilling work of over 300 paged is attested by the fact that it has reached a sixth edition.

" Bunty and the Boys " a story by Helen Attend e, Which originally appeared in a volume of Little Folks, Will be welcomed in book form (Is.) by those who have previously read it, while it will preve a real treat to the boys and girls who see it for the first time. It is a racy story of child life, and is admirably illustrated by Gordon Browne.' In the Sixpenny Series of Cassell's Picture Story Books we have to hand "Nursery Joys for Girls and Boys," "Little Talks with Little People, "Bright Stars," and " Pet's Posy of Pictures and Stories." Every other page of these charming books is illustrated,and the stories are of the most readable and instructive kind. Each volume is bound in cloth; and it is therefore a puzzle how so much that is so good can be given for the money. The Pocket Gazetteer of the World," published by Messrs. John Walker and Co., London, is one of those invaluable handy volumes which every reader should have by his side. It is a distionary of general geography which has been carefully edited by Mr. J. G. Bartholo- mew, F.R.S.E., &c. It briefly answers the questions as to almost every place in the world—" Where is it ?" and "What of it?" There are somel hing like 35,000 references, aed,as everything is brought down to date,it will beseen that preparation of the work has taxed the energies of a considerable number of painstaking writers. By a capital system of abbreviations, a great deal of informa- tion is crowded into ye rf little space. There is a mass of special statistics with regard to the Britielt Empire; but the most interesting feature of the work is a series of beautifully-finished coloured maps illustrating general features ef geography—as follows :-1 height of land, and depth of sea, 2 zones of temperature,3 mean annual rainfall, 4 ocean currents, land surface features, 5 pre- vailing winds, 6 density of population, 7 races of man- kind, 8 the British Empire, and 9 principal routes of commerce. The Pocket Gazetteer is a volume of ever 600 pages ; it is neatly bound, and the price is 2s. Bd. The English Illustrated Magazine (Messrs. Macmillan and Co.) is issued as usual fir Christmas as a double number. It has a high reputation, and that reputation is fully maintained in the current publication. There are no less than a dozen full-page illustrations, to say nothing if minor pictures. The frontispiece, " A study In chalk," from a drawing by C. E. Peragini, is a beauti- ful re-production. The illustrations by W. B. Gardner, to the paper on "Surrey Farm Houses," by Grant Allen, make a series of very pretty pictures ; Mr. Hugh Thomp- son illustrates "The angler's song" in his quaint and humorous fashion; "Macbeth on the stage" is pre- sented in the style of every actor of eminence; and Mr. Herbert Reilton illustrates an article by Mr. R. Owen Allsop in "A Ramble through Norway." Mr. Raton I stands alone in giving the spirit as well as the features of old-time buildings; he has had a great opportunity lin these Normandy studies, and he has excelled himself. ' It should be added that the stories, continued and com- pleted, are worthy of this high-class periodical. Tim "Graphic Christmas Number" is always a feast for the eyes. There are two large coloured presentation plates.; one a reproduction of the painting of "Sweet Ann Page " by G. D. Leslie R.A. : the other is "Juliet, from the picture by P. H. Leslie, RA." Both are from the " Graphic" gallery of Shakespeare's heroines and both are charming—especially "Juliet." Tom Hood's celebrated ballad—" Faithless Nelly Gray" is comically and cleverly illustrated by W. Ralston; there are some striking Indian sketches by Captain E. R. Penrose, illustrating a story by Phil Robinson; and "any number" of picture stories for children, besides the following full-page chromos:—" Should auld acquaint- ance be forgot"' " Twixt two worlds," and the firs' attack. All the illustrations are in colours, and are line spechnensof work of this class. Diprose's Annual has a bright frontispiece showiFX Queen Elizabeth on horseback; it is a reminder of 1588, and the Armada. There are no less than fourteen stories, &c., and more than half of them are strikingly illustrated. Joan Middlemas contributes "Poor Little Neeta York": Howard Paul "An ExcitingeChriatinas" •, F. H. Brame "An Awkward Mistake"; Frederick Warren "A martyr to Science," and the other stories are by more or less notable writers. The Annualis a capital fireside companion d urine the long winter evening. "Our Sunday Nights" (Messrs. Diprose and Bateman) is from the lively pen of Mr. James Greenwood, the I "Amateur Casual.' The sketches originally appeared in "The People," and were so much reled that a demand arose for their issue in book form. Life in London' as seen on Saturday nights, is shown in almost every phase. Mr. Greenwood has a way of edging in where other casuals would fear to go: and ho makes the best use of his eyes and ears. These pictures of social life have &value apart from the immediate pleasure they give, and we can heartily commend the volume to all who recognise that-" the proper study of mankind is man."

"Sharks of Society" is also published by Messrs. Diprose 11.'0 Bateman as a shilling 'volume. It is by Mr. Bracebridge Hemyng,author of " Awful Stories," "Hard Up" There are throe tales; one describes the career of the West end shark; the other that of the domestic shark; and the third narrates the adventures of the marrying shark. Mr. Hemyng has a good (ye for effect in his descriptions; but he is not always careful In the construction of his plots. The volume has plenty of " go," and is sure to find eager readers.

ACCIDENT TO A BALLAST-MAN.—A ballast-man named John Houghton, of Wigan, was working at St. lelens Station on Wednesday afternoon when by some means he got between the buffers. One thigh -was shockingly lacerated and contused, and he was taken to the Provi- dence'Hospital and placed under the care of Drs. Gaskell and O'Brien. LORD HARRINGTON AT HASLINGDEN.—LOM Hartington, addressing a meeting of his constitutents at Haslingden, on Saturday afternoon, said we now knew that Irish members would continue to sit in the Imperial Parlia- ment after the establishment of Home Rule, and he submitted that the Imperial Parliament, having been ousted from all control over affairs exclusively Irish,would have a right to object to the representatives of Ireland having any voice in determining questions exclusively English or Scotch. He strongly objected to the ene man one vote principle, which, in his view, was not a measure of enfranchisement but of disfranchisement. Referring to Mr. Labouchere's remarks about the Duke of Devonshire's property in Ireland, he said there were inaccuracies as to facts, and dealt with charges made against the Liberal Unionist party by Mr. Gladstone at Birmingham. He contended that the Unionists had remained true to Liberal traditions. EXTRAORDINARY BRRACH OF Pitotirse Case.—ln the Queen's Bench Division on Wednesday, before Mr. Baron Huddleeton and a special jury, the trial was begun of an action in which Miss Valery Wiedemann, a German governess, sues Mr. Robert Horace Walpole, heir to the Earldom of Orford, to recover £lO,OOO damages for alleged breach of promise of marriage and for libel. The plaintiff said she met the defendant at an hotel in Constantinople, and he proposed marriage to her. The next evening she was sitting at a window when the defendant suddenly entered the room and forcibly seduced her. He afterwards renewed his 'promise of marriage and gave her a signet ring. She subsequently gave birth to a boy, and she brought this action on hear- ing that the defendant was married. The alleged libel was a statement by the defendant that she had stolen the ring. In cross-examination the plaintiff said she usually resided in Vienna, but sometimes in Rome. The case was adjourned.—On Thursday, on the resump- tion, the plaintiff refused to answer questions regard- ing the date of the child's birth and the time she beCAMS peegnant, and said that if the questions were pressed she would not proceed. Baron Huddleston thereupon pro- nounced judgment for the defendant.—The "Pall Mall Gazette" understands that notice of motion for a new trial is about to be served at once on the ground that the plaintiff, being a foreigner and not understanding the procedure of the English courts, did not realise the consequences which would follow her refusal to answer. The application will, come before two judges in the Divisional Court.

FOOTWALKS LI RUNCORN. Sir,—Some years ago there was an order issued by the Commissioners that the footwallts.in Duke's Field should , be tiled or flagged. As an owner of property lat once complied. There are, however, quite a number in' Lower Bentinck, Leinster, and Bra.ckley streets not yet completed, and I vrish to know why.? The cellar grids are flagged round and stand abave the beaten cinders about two inches, a most dangerous state of affairs this eason of the year. The property 6s. well tenanted. I question whether the landlord could claim his rent owing to the approaches being left in such a.,..;on- dition. Let the Commissioners see to it, and at ouce, and deal fair play all round.—Yours, INJURED. Nov. 28th, 1888.
COUNTY COIJNOIL.

..Sir,—From the number of-C-aldicia:tes for our new geouncil we may, I hope, augur weU for its future .efficiency, if the electorate will take a little care and -allow discrimination in the choice of representatives. We, as electors, have a duty to perform, and the difficulty *eons to be in rural divisions like Apple on ,aud flares- bury, to get an expression of opinion frotn new areas sv,bech have not been called upon before to act together. It.oecurs to me that this may be attained by the over- seers .of each township summoning a meeting of the ratepeyers, to elect two or more delegates who would meet hose from the other townships in the division, and discuss the question of a suitable and representative man wiBing to stand. The recommendation of such a ' body woald of course bind no one, but the man of their choice weuld come with great weight before the zon= stituency, and in this way the trouble and cost of a contest wzmad probably be avoided, to the advantage of the ratepwrs who under the provisions of the Act are responsible for the chief part of the expenses. The Farmers' Club have, I see, met and considered the qllBB- - and, as it due to so important an interest, seek to have a share of direct representation on the Couny Board, but we must remember that there are other ireerests among us besides the agricultural, and it is in the hope that I trtty do something to bring about a free expression of opinion on this important matter, that I /nave thought it rigLz to ask for the insertion of this appeal to my co-electors, as no time is to be lost.—l am, yours respectfully, WILLIAM LONG. • Tholwall Heys, near Warrington, Nov. 28th, 1888. A TEETOTALLER LX A "FIX.".. Sir,—llaving a strong bias in favour of temperance, and even of teetotalism, I have been rather staggered by some conclusions which have been come to by a prominent French statistician, M. de Flaix, itho has been collecting figures bearing on Gte influence of alcohol on morality and health. "M de Flaix finds," we are told," that in those departments of France where the - consumptien of alcohol is small, the birth-rate is less, and the mortality greater than in other parts of the Republic. Comparing different nations he points out that in France, which consumes less alcohol than the United Kingdom' this birth rate is less, the mortality higher, and the criminality and suicide rates much greater. Italy consumes very little alcohol, but its criminality is appallidg. Spain, however, which con- sumes three times less alcohol than Italy has doubts the _

amount of crime. Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, with a population of about one-third, consume four times the quantity of alcohol consumed in Italy, and yet the criminality of the former is small while that of the latter is appalling.' According to the figures given by M deFlaix the consumption of alcohol is in direct corralatioa with the amount of crime in the countries pplpared, and he, therefore, assumes that the use of alcohol is procTuciiiii of morality and virtue, and abstention from its use provocative of crime and immorality." I confess, sir, that I had always religiously believed that all the virtues were on the side of total abstinence, and I had never suspected that such good-looking credentials could be put in on the other side. Perhaps there are some amongst your readers who can re-assure one who doesn't like to hear alcohol well spoken of.—l am, sir, yours tce., WAVERER.

GOVERNMENT AND THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir,—l should esteem it a favour if you will kindly Terni!t insert iii the t.y.olupins of your valuable paper a few of my i:ltotiggsto the advocafes of teetotal- I !FT% ernieavouring to show them the injury they have ' inflicted upon the intemperate part of the community by their action in opposing the county measure which had, for one of its objects, the laudable one of giving the people pormiision to buy up any public-houses or dram shops which they thought useless. Now I think in their opposition to the above scheme they have shoWn themselves both narrow-minded, unjust, and thoughtless, and have damped the Govern- ment's exertions in the direction of temperance reform.

In the first place, the teetotal advocates must never txpect an English Government—composed of the most common-sense and practical men that the nation can send to be its law makers—to pass laws which shall have for their object the purpose of placing a small minority of business men at the mercy of a number of fanatics, 'who have- shown by. their disposition to be void of common-sense and justice, for I believe no man who has a grain of justice in his nature would think of taking from another his business and living without giving compensation. What they take to do otherwise would be robbery of the clearest description, for at no time in the annals of English history cad we point to any such act of robbery_ Now, by opposing the measure, the teetotal fanatics show that they consider a few thousand pounds of more consequence than the . social and moral welfare of their fellow-creatures, for to what a useful purpose might we have put the hotels or public-houses so purchased ? We might have turned them into neat and clean tempe- rance hotels. It would have paid as an investment and would have been a serious rival to the remaining gin palaces, and the saloon—for I say the coffee-shops of to-day are not sufficient to counteract the influence of the gin palaces and public-houses. I say they drive men to, instead of taking them from, the public-house. We want to do less talking and more practical work. If the teetotal fanatic will not allow the Government to spend its money for the benefit of temperance—why not each and every denomination in the town work and buy up a public-house? We should very soon lessen the amount of evil. A temperance society with business notions would buy up and close public-houses in quar- ters where they are not wanted for public convenience, and not likely to be re-opened for individual interest. I say a temperance society not eaten up by ready-made denunciations and with its eyes open would have a tem- perance hotel, and devise rules and regulations for its management. The public would like them; the com- mercial travellers would Sock to them ; and an organiza- tion might be established which would be self-support- ing, and diffuse temperance principles by making them respected as words of health, power, morals, and comfort. W. FURNESS. Poplars, Great Sankey.

POLICE NEWS. At Hddisbury Petty Sessions on Monday, before a full bench of magistrates, the following cases were heard : ALLEGED ASSAULT.—A case in which George Jackson, of Prodsham. was summoned by Mary Southern, of the same place, for assaulting her on the 27th October, was dismissed. Mr. W. H. Chorton defended.—ln a case arising out of this one, in which Ellen Howard was summoned by Catherine Mercer for assaulting her at Frodsham on the same day, a fine of Si. and costs was imposed. Mr. Churton again, appeared for the defence. MODERN CELEBRATORS OF TILE Pmts.—Sohn Clarke and Harry Miller, summoned for letting of fireworks at Prodsham, were discharged with a caution:—Samuel Caldwell, who did not appear, was ordered to pay the costs 4s. ed. for a similar offence. _

CLAIM FOR WAGES.—John Challinor. farmer, Froclsham Lordship, was summoned by an Irish farm labourer, named Michael Callaghan, for £1 88. Ifid., wages due.—Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich. defended.— It appeared the claim was for balance of moneialleged fly complainant to be owing him for picking potatoes.—After hearing the evidence, the Bench decided that under the agreement the defendant had no right to any money, and they dismissed the case. TIELVY FINE FOR AIDING POACHERS,—Sarah Btirkhill, an elderly woman, of Frodsham, was summoned for having on toe 27th October aided and abetted poachers, Mr. Fletcher defended. Mr. Cooke appeared on behalf of the police, and on his statement it seemed that at half-past eight on the morning in question P. C. Pearson who had been watching the defendant's house, saw a man named eice go up to the door with a horse and cart. Defendant went out and spoke to him, and afterwards returned to the inside of the house. She again appeared in a few minutes, bringing two baskets velsich contained something, and they were put in the cart. Rice then went on, and defendant followed some distance. P.C. Pearson then left his hiding place, and asked Mrs. Burkhill what was in the cart. She said some rabbits, and they were being taken .to the station. She was then asked where she had got them from, and she said from a man named Thomas Bradbury, of Salop, and that they had come to Frodsham station. The police had made inquiries since, and found that no rabbits had come to Frodsham station for Mrs. Burkhill for some time, and he (Mr. Cooke) would prove distinctly that they had been pouched. Evidence in support of this state- ment was given by P.C. Pearson, a railway official at Trod- sham, and a farm servant named Grice.—The defendant was fined £5 and costs, and was allowed a week in which to pay the money.—Rdward Lightfoot, for a similar offence at Tarvin on the 3rd November, was fined 30s. and costs, on the evidence of Sergeant Crabbe. • Mr. Churton defended.—John Arrowsrnith and Thomas Arrowsraith for a similar offence, in Brinbury, on the same day. and Ann Schofield, for a similar Offenee,in Kingsley,on the 6th November, were fined 20s. and 10a. costs respectively. The cases were proved by P.C. Bate and P.C. Marshall.—Mr. Cooke prosecuted on behalf of the police in each case.

Hill and Grundy, shipowners, &c., of St. Helens and Sankey Bridges. The phiintiff claimed from the defendants for damages sustained to his flat, Thorn, and the cargo in the same, through the negligence of the defendants' servants on board his fiat The Hearts of Oak, whereby his fiat ran into the Thorn while lying aground on Thursday, the 6th September, i 1888, n the Mersey between Widnes and Hale Head. The particulars of damages were: Damage to fiat Thorn, £lO 3. 5d.: damages to cargo, .£lO 3s. 7d.' • loss of service from September 18th to October 10th, 1888, £8; total £2B 'TEL—Mr. T. Swift, barrister (instructed by Mr. John W. Knowles, solicitor, Widnes). appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pickier& barrister (instructed by. Messrs'. Grandy and Lamb, solicitors, Manchester), were for the defendants.— It appeared that the flat Thorn left Widnes on Septem- ber 6th, 1888, with a cargo of saltcake for Liverpool. Alm Massey was in charge. When near Hale Head site ran aground, and the Heart of Oak was then about two hundred yards behind, and as Massey saw the danger that was impending he called out to the captain of defendant's fiat tootake another tack, as he was aground. DROWNING CASES AT RUNCORN. GALLANT CONDUCT OF A BROTHER.

flatman named Henry Moores was drowned in the river Mersey at Runcorn on Thursday evening. ..hhout six o'clock, the deceased and his brother Robert went down to the Dock near the Ferry with the intention of going to a flat, that lay agrsund on a -sandbank. The deceased went and obtained a small boat, and was sculling it to the side of a flat moored alongside the wall for the purpose of taking his brother on board, when he overbalanced himself and fell into the water. Robert at once jumped into the water to the aid of his brother, and he succeeded in seizing his hand, but the tide was running fast, and he lost his hold. The de- ceased disappeared, and Robert came out of the water. In a few moments one of the spectators of the scene shouted "There he is," and Robert acrain bravely dived into the water, but his efforts to find °his brother were in vain_ The dead body was recovered near the Ferry Hut about two o'clock yesterday morning. The deceased, who was a young maa of 24 years, was married and had a wife residing at Salford. On the same evening a Ship Canal labourer, named Patrick23rennan, was drowned in the Weston Canal opposite Weston Point Docks. It appears that Brennan left the uke of Wellington Hotel, Runcorn, about 8 o'clock in company with a man named Jas. Gough. He was then sober, and Crough saw him commence to walk along the kanal side towards Weston Point. Afterwards Thomas McLean, a young man, who was sauntering along withthis sweetheart heard cries of distress issuing from the leek near the iron bridge, and on returning to the spot he ,saw a mac struggling in the water. He quickly obta:iped a buoy from the watchman's but, and threw it to the drowning man, but he was too exhausted to take advantage of this help, and sank. The dead body was reassered and now lies at the Weaver Hotel awaiting an in9uest. The deceased is apparently about 45 years of age.

before anything could be done the Thorn was struck on the starboard quarter and her rudder was smashed. The force of the collision threw Massey into the river, nd his small boat was cut away. On being picked out e the war heaw the Heart df Oak sailing away. He shouted ontto those on the other flat to bring the boat back, as his flat was making water, but no answer was given. Manley ran his-flat ashore,on Frodsharti Marsh and caulked the stern post a bit, and on arriving at Alexandra deck, Liverpool, a•few days after, it was found that 117 tons of the cargo was damaged, and it was returned to Messrs. Sullivan and Co., at Widnes. Numerous witnesses were called in support of these facts. Mr. Fickford, for the defence, contended, that they were not responsible for all the eaulking that was done, because part of thatwas done bystraining on the bank. and if they took longer time than-was neeessiry to do the repairs they could not charge them for the lose of time occasioned.- .They had said they lost-, throe tripsi but. thatwas,not the defendants' fault, as it was through not getting the work done quicker. Only two things could have been done—one was to help the man out of the water, and -the other was-to get the boat which was floating away. 3Lr. Pickford pointed out that they were only fifteen yards from them when the man was got eat of the water, and preparation were ,being made to reach the boat when they saw it was being picked up by the captain of the Alice. They must also understand ,that the plaintiff's flat went aground quite stupidly right under his client's bows.—Mr. Swift pointed out thatan offer had been made to pay for the rudder, which showed that The defendants admitted liability: and the person who was liable to pay for the rudder, was liable to pay for the whole of the injuries. —The jury, which had boon empannelled to hear the case, returned a wardiet for the plaintiffs fer the full amount of the first two items ' and for £4 for the less of the flat's services to Mr. Higham, making a total of £24 7s. Costs were allowed.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. 13%, ARIEL." That it is regretted that the endeavours of •the Widnes Free Library Committee to progide intellectual amusement for the public do not meet with more general recognition. That crimes of violence (war in Widnes in appall- ing frequency. It would not be beyond the mack to say that cases of wounding have averaged at least one a week for the past six months, the wife in many instances being the victim of her husband's brutality. _

That the sentences passed upon the offenders do not seem to have a deterrent erect upon others, who evidently give too much play to their passions and too little to their reason. That one is forced to the conclusion that Widnes is indeed a "black spot' and apparently is likely to remain so. Can an answer be supplied to this conundrum? What influence has the dull and dreary surroundings of the majority of the houses in Widnes in making not only men, toit women, brutish and vicious?
That much enthusiasm was displayed at the Wesleyan temperance meeting on Thursday even- ing, and a crusade against drink is not unlikely to be, th e outcome.

That the County Council continues to be an interesting topil of conversation. That Mr. Brundrit has formally offered his services to the electors of Runcorn South, in an address which sets forth his fitness for the position he seeks in modest terms.

That were present appearances to be the guide, it might be predicted that Mr. Brundrit will be returned unopposed. That in Runcorn North matters are evidently to be very lively and the 2,500 electors will have plenty of choice. That Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sen., will probably be asked to represent Widnes, on the County Council, and failing him, Mr. E. K. Maspratt will be invited to fill the position.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY—The usual weekly meeting of this society was held in the Drill Hall, on Monday, when Mr. A. T. Gillanders read a paper on "Life History of a Tree." A short discussion followed. SPECIAL SERMON'S AT TNE PARISH CIIIIRCH.—OR Sun- day special sermons were preached in the above place of worship by the Rev. F. H. Reichardt, M.A., incumbent of St. Thomas', Madras, on behalf of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—The anniversary services in connection with the Primitive Methodist chapel were held on Sunday, when sermons were preached afternoon and evening by Rev. G. F. Taylor, from Canada, to good congregations. Collections were taken on behalf of the trust funds.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL—The anniversary services in connection with this chapel were held on Sunday, when sermons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. , George Dickenson, of Mytholmroyd. The subject of the morning discourse wc.s taken from Hebrews iv.l4-16, and in the evening from Psalm cxxxiii. The congregations were good, fair collections being realized. TEA MEETING AND LECTURE.—On Monday evening 3 public tea meeting was held in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, Eagle Brow. Tea was provided at 5.30, the following ladies presiding at the tables: --Mesdames Evans, Edwards, Thomasson, and Appleton. About 100 sat down to tea, after which the Rev. G. F. Taylor delivered his popular lecture on "Canadian Life,' the chair being occupied by Mr. Jas. Dodds. At the close of the lecture a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer, on the proposition of Mr. Thomason, seconded by Mr. G. L. Welforer. About £lB was realized from the services and lectures. HEATLEY AND DISTRICT HARRIERS.—The opening run of this club took place on Saturday from the Railway Hotel, Heatley (the headquarters of the club), 10 mem- bers turning out. At 3.5 the hares, W. Travis and F. 11 mop, were despatched with the trail, followed four minutes later by the slow pack, consisting of B. Harrop, A. Sca tergood, H. Taylor, and W. Johnson, they in turn being followed four minutes later by the fast pack, F. Taylor (captain), pace, T. Travis, J. Scattergood, and H. Trenor. The trail ran along the road till the Bailin was crossed into Warburton, and then over the fields to Cave Green and Dunham Massey, crossing the Bollin again by the wooden bridge and threw+' the meadows to Bollington, one of the pack getting a duck- ing in attempting to jump a broad stream. The slow pack were here overtaken. The trail next ran through Agden to Simpson's farm, where the trail gave out, and the captain giving the word to go a splendid race home resulted in F. Taylor winning by three yards from T. Travis, J. Scattergood third, the rest close up, an enjoyable run of about six miles occupying some 40 minutes. WESLEYAN MISSIONARY Masriso.—The annual sermons in aid of Foreign Missions were preached by the Rev. George Dickenson, in the Wesleyan Chapel, Lymm, on Sunday, to a large congregation.—On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held. Mr. Joseph Thoip occupied he chair, being supported by the Revs. George Dickenson, G. E. Young, W. Brookes, and Mr. Ashton. After a short service the Rev. Wm. Brookes read the report, which showed that the society, besides having missions in Ireland, America, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Austria, was having noble work done by a band of ladies who were working among the women of the East. The income of the parent society was, last year, £131,867 2s. 6d., the expenditure was £137,967 3s. 10d., leaving a deficiency of £6,100 7s. 9d. That deficiency added to that of former years showed the present deficiency at the end of last year to be £16,859 7s. Bd. Towards the total receipts the Warrington circuit had raised £298 ss. Of that amount, £lOO had been given by the " Sunlight " Soap Company. Warrington raised £Bl 16a.; Penketh £l7 15s. lid. ; Moore £2O 4s. 7d. ; Whitley £5 18s. 2d.; Antrobus £6 4s. ld. ; Appleton £7' 2s. ; Padgate £lB ; Hatton £4 2s. sd. ; Latchford £7 Is. 2d. ; Martinscroft £1 17s. Bd. ; Sankey Bridges £8 3s. ed. ; Lyn= £lB 19s. 6d. (Applause.)—The Rev. G. E. Young then addressed the meeting. Nothing, he said, could meet the needs of the world but the Gospel preached by the Holy Ghost, sent down from heaven. Notwithstanding the difficulties which beset the path of the Missionary Society, they had reason to feel very much encouraged because victory was on their side. (Hear, hear.) They were on the right track, and success would attend their efforts, for God was on their side.—The Rev. George Diekenson also delivered an address upon the progress of missionary work, after which the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

• Mr. Gladstone has made handsome present of books to Chester free library. Sir Henry Norman, governor of J ' amaica has been appointed to the vacant governorship of Queensland, about which there has been so much talk. _

Dr. Watson, arbi,rator in the Noriri.a England iron works claim, has issued his decision. He grants the men 6d. per ton on puddling, and 5 per cent, on other wages. MR. Bnioarr's ILLNESS.—At eleven yesterday morning, Dr. Hayle arrived at One Ash, and at twelve he issued this bulletin :—" Mr. Bright has passed a tolerably fair night. The state of the lung and his general condition is just the same as yesterday." The Select Committee appointed by the House of Commons to inquire into the alleged breach of privilege by Sergeant Sullivan met again on Friday, the Home Secretary presiding. The proceedings, which were private, were again adjourned. COLLISION IN BRISTOL CHANNEL.—A, collision. occurred on Thursday in Bristol Channel, off Longships, between the steamers Hoopoe, of Cork, from Liverpool to Ant- werp, and the Sir Galahad, of Swansea. The Hoopoe sank, and a seaman named peter and a passenger named Nelsonwere drowned. The remainder were landed at Penarth. The Sir Galahad put back to Swansea. A PIT ON FIRE.—TEREE MEN DEAD.—One of Messrs. Ainsworth's iron ore pits at Cleator is on fire. Yesterday morning three men went down the pit to inspect, and were suffocated in the smoke. ,The dead body of John Mills, of Cleator, has been got Mit. James Phillips and M'Avoy are still in the pit. They must be dead. Attempts were made to get at them, but the rescuers were driven back by smoke. Crowds are on the pit top, and great excitement prevails. LOUD SALISBURY AT EDINBURGH.—In the Edinburgh Corn Exchange, yesterday, Lord Salisbury, in the pres- ence of 6,000 persons, was presented with .500 addresses from Conservative and Liberal Unionist associations, in Scotland, representing 62 constituencies. The Marquis of Salisbury, acknowledging the addresses, said the duty imposed upon the Conservative and Liberal Unionist party in Scotland might be expressed in these two words —organise and teach—so that they might act as one party, having one mind, on the on great qtiestion Which was the question of the moment. The result of the Holborn election he regarded as a very valuable indica- tion of public opinion. Upon the issue of the struggle— whether they could maintain the unity of the two islands or not—depended the integrity of the Empire which they all loved so well.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock.

QuitsrloNs, 14c.—Baron Worms intimated Sir Henry Norman has been appointed Governor of Queensland.— The Lord Advocate said no adequate grounds existed for granting free pardon, or compensation, to Hugh Matheson of Clastmore sent to prison for rioting, but hehad since been liberated.- • SUPPLY AC.—The House went in Committee of tipply. The Civil Service Estimates vote for superanuation and retired allowances was under consideration. Mr. H. Fowler drew attention to principles which regulate granting pensions:and also to defective administration under which pensions had been granted. The Chancellor of the Exchequer said Government, in adopting recom- mendations of commission would require the support of the House of Commons. The Government agreed with the recommendations of the commission, and woulditake steps to give effect to them by legislation if neccessary. Lord R. Churchill regarded the statement of the Chancellor of the Exchequer as highly satisfactory and encouraging.—Mr. Brunwaran, Sir G. CAMPBELL, and Mr. HANBURY condemned the system that enabled persons like Mr. Clifford Lloyd to secure a pension. The discussion was continued by Mr. Laubouchere, Mr. Esselmont, Mr. Conybeare, and Dr. Tanner. [LEFT SITTING).

CHANGE OF CURATES AT THE PARISH CHURCH.-, The Rev, T.-A. Easterling, one of the curates at the Warrington Parish Char* preached his farewell sermon to a large congregation on Sunday evening last. Mr. Easterling is leaving Warrington for Jersey. We understand that the Rev. James E. Hand, curate of St. Andr,m's, Hadfield, Derbyshire, has been appointed to the curacy at the Parish Church. LORD SALISAURT n SCOTLAND.—The Marquis of Salis- bury began his campaign in Midlothian on Thursday by addressing a crowded meeting in the Edinburgh Corn Exchange. He received a very enthusiastic welcome. The Duke of Buccleugh presided. The Premier began by lamenting that some Scotch measures whichthe Govern- ment strongly desired to pass had disappeared from the Order book of the Heti.* of Commons, but he attributed that result to systetnatic obstruction in the House. Dealing then with 'the questions of the day, he complained that no practical result had 'followed the great meeting at Birmingham. In the proposals of Home Rule what Loyalists had to fear was not legislation but that the executive government should fall into " rebel " hands. He alleged that reland, if in the hands of an enemy would be an over- whelming danger—a danger for the commercial ports in this country. It was impossible to think that separation would tend to soften the hearts of the people of Ireland to England. In conclusion, the Premier said it was to Scotland they all looked, and the moment Scotland realised the real danger which threatened the loyalists, their fellow-religionists, in Ireland, then Home Rule would be dead: Tills PARNELL Istetrinv.—At the Parnell Commission on Tuesday,Sergeant Gilhooly, who in 1879 and for some years subsequently was stationed at Castleisland, said there were no outrages in Castleisland before the estab- lishment of the Land League. In cross-examination he admitted that a book calledan " outrage-book" was kept, and Sir Charles Russell asked that this book be pro- duced. The( Commissioners ruled:that everything should be produced which Could throw any light upon the case, and Sir Charles Russell said he would reserve further cross-examination until the book was in court. Inspec- tor William Davies then gave evidence, in the course of which he said the police force of Castleisland was in- creased from seven men toile) after the establishment:of the League. There was a central Moonlighting organisa- tion in Dublin. He refused to disclose the name of his Informant. Sergeant Gilhooly (recalled) produced a book containing a list of the outrages in the Castleisland district in 1879. In the course or the afternoon Sir Charles Russell made application for a further discovery of documents in the possession of the "Times," particu- larly letters alleged to have been written-by Mr. Devitt and Mr. O'Kelly. Judgment on this matter was reserved. On Wednesday Thomas Galvin spoke of an attack upon 'Ms hOuse at Castleisland in 1880-; when he was offered the alternative of being shot or having his ears cut off. He chose to be shot, and was wounded in the thigh. In cross-examination he said he believed the outrage was the result of a:family dispute. Later in the day, Joanne Brown, a widow, narrated the circumstances of the murder of her husband in 1882 by Barrett and Poff, who were executed. Several other witnesses were called, and the inquiry was then` adjourned. On Thursday seeseral persons who lied been injured by moonlighters were examined. Inspector Crane gave evidence as to the prevalence of crime in county Kerry from the time of the establishment of the Land League, and said that wherever the League was started outrages followed, and the League never gave the police any assistance.— District Inspector Rice, recalled, said he never before the formation of the Land League knew of people being denounced in Listowel for taking evicted farms. Another I witness was Mary Reap, of Drimoleague, county Cork, who deposed to the murider of her father by moonlighters for taking an evicted farm. Yesterday Mr. Samuel Hussey the well known Kerry landlord and land agent, gave evidence. He said he had carried out a member of evictions for non-payment of rent, but he believed the tenant in each could have paid. He first heard of moon- lighting in 1880. Previous to then the only secret society he had ever heard of was the Fenian Society. Jeremiah Haggerty deposed that he had been boycotted by the League, and had lost £16,000 in consequence. 4The Court adjourned until Tuesday. CHRSHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE APrLETON :LamEs AND GTiNTLKAULN,—A. Witsk having been expressed thittNl should offer myself as a Candidate for the Appleton Division of the County Council, I 'beg to offer my services, 'add at the same time to assure the Ratepayers that, if they honour me with their saffrages, 'it -would be my it rnest desire to promote the interests of the County, and specially of the Appleton Division, by 'every.means in my power, and to give careful attention to the duties of the position which I may be elected to fill. Raving been for some years a member of the Finance Committee, and other- vise conversant with County business, I trusti may be con- sidered competent to represent and to watch over your interests in this very important And responsible Council. I 'have the honour to be, Yours dalthfully, J. CIIARIMON PARR. Grappenhall Reyes, Warrington, Nov. 22nd,11.2813.

COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE APPLETON DIVISION IN THE COUNTY OF CHESTER. LADIES NO GENTLEISEX.—Agt-the urgent request of a large number of Electors interested in Agricultural ,and Industrial' pursuits, I have consented to stand as -.a Candidate to represent you in the County 'Crunch. My whole life has been spent amongst those-whose interests are mainly affected by the expenditure undenthe control of the County Authorities. My highest aim would be to protect those interests, and, whilst endeavouring to promotevinciency in the administra- tion of County affairs, an effort must also be male to lessen the burden of taxation which new presses so'keavily on the Agriculturist and those engaged In Industrial purstilta. To attain that object my time, experience, and. energies will be at your disposal ; and no one feels more keenly than I do the necessity of the AgricuLttsral interests, and Aliso those of the Industrial classes, being reyeesented by men of prac- tical and tried experience. These are the grounds upon which I solicit your support, and, if returned to represent you, no effort will be wanting on my part to retain the confidence wig& you will have reposed in me. I am, Your obedient Servant, *Old Farm, Appleton. JOSEPH -KNOWLES.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE •FRODS.UO,3I DIVISION. LADIFS AIM IiNTLEMEAT,--Havlag received several gratifying requisitions from the Electorate of this Division. representingall classes and every shade of opinion. I beg to offer myself as your representative in the County Council to be elected in January next. I have gained experience in public work, in the various offices I have held in this Union during the last twenty years, and have been Justice of the Peace for this county for twelve years. I was in business as a tenant farmer and =tanner in this. Union all the early part of my life, thus having a sound practical training in ordinary affairs, and was also by this means drawn into intimate and pleasant association with the labouring classes. .1 have the needful leisure to attend to public wotk.aaci have no private interests to serve, of my own or any one else. tl am strongly of opinion that the Council should be non- , political. - ' "Oh fatal day! Oh, day for over curet I Thus to be forced at this unhappy time. Upon a choice of cruelty, or crime; But sooner let Dick Horner die with pain (Hard though the thought), and Robin's nose remain. His beauteous corpse, yet bright with manhood's bloom, ' Shall go unmutilated to the tomb. . Heaven knows my heart is tortured with the thought, In life I did not use him as I ought; • And must I aggravate the guilt I feel, And deseorats his body with the steel? Could my warm tears his generous life recall, From morn to night the drops of grief should fall. Could my.deep sighs again renew his breath, • But for one year, rd sigh myself to death. Could he but live, and live with me once more, I'd show a nobler conduct than before. Oh, could he live !—but Nature's laws forbid— I'd use him vastly better than I did." Thus, as she long lamented in the place, She kissed him aft, and 'wept upon his face, Till the salt tears so tickled on his skin, From very angiiish, lie was foreettogrin. "He lives! he moves! new life his body warms!" The lady cried, and clasped him in her arms. Help soon was summoned by the excited wife,' And baths and chafing brought him back to life. So, now to bring my story to a date, I hasten on; it Just remains to state That Dick recovered from his strange attack, And all his wonted health and strength came back. That Robin and his wife were friendiu,of course; That Lila put her geod resolves in force; And soon became, beneath this altered plan, The prudent partner of.a happy man. The uncle died, as all rich uncles ought. And left to Lila all the wealth he'd got. Their prospects rose, which, ere-while, were'so bad, And both were kind, and both were mighty glad— Glad:as the cow, that leaps and lifts her tail, When a warm spring renews the grassy vale.
